speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to raise a question of privilege having to do with a Canadian Press dispatch which appears in this morning's Montreal Gazette and probably has been published in other Canadian papers. The heading of the article is "Stiffer Attitude Seen in Outlays for Vets." The article goes on to say:

A stiffening attitude towards further financial outlays through allowances for Canada's veterans is reflected in rejection by the veterans committee of two new proposals.
It adds this paragraph, which is the one about which I am complaining:
The Department of Veterans Affairs recommended that student-veterans at universities be given a $5 a week commutation allowance if they had to travel a certain distance to school and a $5 a month textbook allowance. The committee rejected both but accepted a loan plan to aid such veterans.
As a matter of fact no such proposal was put before the committee on veterans affairs by the Department of Veterans Affairs, and that paragraph of the report is entirely erroneous.
Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Veterans Affairs): I entirely agree with my hon. friend.

Because of the desire to get the bill into committee we did not raise any objection at that time. As a matter of fact no remarks were made when the order was called for second reading. But as we in this group look over this bill and find that its important provisions are for increases of salaries, many of which are already quite large, we do not take kindly to it. The lowest salaries referred to in the bill, aside from salaries for part-time service, are of the order of $5,000, which are to be increased to $6,666.66. Then they go all the way up to a present salary of $15,000, which is to become $20,000. I know that some of us hold a view which other hon. members of the house do not understand, but we still feel that when old age pensioners are asked to live on the amounts provided them, when the suggestion is made that a ten cents an hour increase is all that should be granted to workers at this time, it is not fair to propose such munificent increases in salaries in brackets that are already so high.
I have no objection to large salaries; I have no objection to judges, but we should look at this matter in- the proper perspective. I am all for the dignity of our courts and our judiciary, but too much emphasis has been laid upon the necessity of large salaries to maintain that dignity. One must also bear in mind that there are generous pension provisions in the act for judges and their widows. Taken by themselves, I have no objection to salaries of this kind being provided, but in the light of our failure in this parliament to deal properly with old age pensioners, which I mention particularly, it is hardly called for. I know that at times when we on this side of the house have made reference to what has been done for old age pensioners as compared with some of these large salaries we get replies from the other side to the effect that it is "cheap stuff", and so on. I suggest that that is not so. If the word "dignity" has any merit or validity, it applies to all citizens, and one has to ask the question how much dignity can be maintained on an old age pension of $25 a month. It does seem to me that the Minister
of Justice, as a member of a government which has failed to deal properly with our old age pensioners, has a tough proposition on his hands to make a case for the increases set out in this bill.

speechtext:
I wish to say a few words on this section. I had intended to say them on second reading of the bill. This bill is one of the most important ones we have before parliament. For many years the Judges Act has remained a dead letter, as to the function of judges, the appointment to their offices, and so on. We should have an equitable system of appointing judges. There should be an amendment to the act in that respect. Some judges in the Montreal district are classed as superior court judges and they are doing the very same work as is done by His Honour Judge Barker, the able senior judge of the county of York. He has the largest number of civil and other cases in any industrial area in Canada.
I had two bills before the house which the minister said he would consider, but I do not see any reference to them in this legislation. One dealt with judges, providing that they should not serve on what are known as federal commissions. Unless we have too many judges their time should be fully occupied with judicial and not parliamentary matters. We are fast building up in this country a system of commission government over the head of parliament when it is in session. The other bill related to the construction to be placed upon certain statutes, providing that a decision of a court of record on authoritative cases shall be final and binding, and shall be followed by all judges appointed under this act. I find that is not the case now. In one particular matter which has been referred to many times in this house we find that the decision of the final court, the judicial committee of the privy council, which should be authoritative and binding Upon all judges appointed under the Judges Act, was not followed, though there can be no doubt about the law in that connection.
I am sorry to see that some of the recommendations of the chief constables' association are not implemented in this legislation. I do not want to speak very long, since this is our first morning session, but since confederation the federal government has not enforced its own laws. Every year hundreds of orders in council and acts are passed by this parliament, but the federal government does nothing to enforce them. Their enforcement is left to the attorneys general of the nine provinces. It is the duty of the federal government to enforce its own laws. All these acts are passed under
Judges Act

section 91 of the British North America Act, and their enforcement should be under fhe federal government instead of being handed over to the provinces, who in turn delegate it to the municipalities, who have to pay the costs. With the tens of thousands of orders in council passed during the war, this has placed an intolerable burden upon every municipal police system in the country. Last Saturday we had a meeting in the city of Toronto of chief constables from many cities on both sides of the border; we had the police games, and all that sort of thing. There is also a chief constables' association. Why was their brief not included here? I remember when I was head of the city council and police commissioner in Toronto the police chiefs of many cities met there and formed the Canadian chief constables' association. These men are out day and night, meeting all kinds of people, many of whom come across the border and commit all sorts of offences here, while the public are not protected.
There is another matter I am sorry is not dealt with in this legislation. I had a return brought down showing the large number of people killed and injured in fatal accidents on the highways. There were twenty-seven killed or injured last week end, and it is the same throughout the year. The province can spend sixty or seventy thousand dollars in prosecuting a person charged with culpable homicide, but it has not a dollar to spend to deal with this menace. More people are injured in the city of Toronto each year than would fill the seats in this House of Commons ten times over. In my city alone thousands of people were injured by the motor car, constituting one of Canada's greatest scandals.	Men, women and children are
slaughtered. Small children lawfully using the streets are struck down by hit and run drivers, and what are we doing to stop it? We are doing nothing under this bill. The penalties should be increased. That offence should be considered culpable homicide to a preeminent degree, because as I have said before nothing is so cowardly as that particular offence.
Now may I say a word about the appointment of judges. I do not wish to advocate the American system, of electing judges- more care in selection is needed-but with all respect I think the minister should tell us who makes these appointments of county court judges. The other day I made some remarks about members of the bar which I am afraid the right hon. attorney general, who was very patient, misunderstood. All appointments made to the county court of York are lawyers of at least ten years stand-

ing at the bar, but I had in mind that some of them had not practised for many years. They may have been county clerks or township clerks or division court clerks, or held some other municipal office before being appointed to the county court bench. I am not saying the men appointed have not been good men, but I believe there should be some better system of appointment. It has been a rule since confederation that members of the House of Commons shall not ask the right hon. attorney general, who is Minister of Justice, to give legal opinions to the house or the committees thereof. That is a wise rule, because he is Attorney General of Canada, and- there may be contests in the law courts between him and the attorneys general of the provinces. But I believe we should know ihow these appointments are made. I understand the provincial and federal cabinet ministers make recommendations to the minister. Sir John A. Macdonald appointed members of both parties to the bench, which had a good effect. He appointed some people who were on the opposite side of politics, because after all is said and done, our system is different from that of the mother country. Our Department of Justice includes the equivalent of four or five departments of the government in England. It performs the functions of the attorney general; it performs the functions of the solicitor general; it carries out the duties of the lord chancellor in England, who appoints the judges and is responsible for their salaries and the conduct of their offices. In addition our Minister of Justice has under his jurisdiction our penal institutions, which in England come under the home secretary. So in Canada this department has grown to be very important. The present minister is probably one of the best lawyers we have ever had in this office. A great many eminent lawyers have held this position, and I am filled with a spirit of deep humility when I recall some of them and their fine work for Canada.
The war has been over for a year, but we have not had a commission appointed to revise the criminal code. One provision of the code is violated every day, the provision concerning who may wear certain clothing and who may not. That is only a small matter, but there are other sections of the code which need to be looked into. In this connection I am sorry to say that one matter, which is now before the court of appeal in Ontario, was mentioned in this high court of parliament. That should not have been done, because the matter is still pending before the courts of the province of Ontario.

Judges Act
Then I understand the attorney general of Ontario wrote a letter to the Attorney General of Canada asking for certain changes in the law regarding culpable homicide. I have been trying to get something done about motor cars and many other matters, but I find no action has been taken on all these matters. Then I think we should have some explanation from the Attorney General about the recommendations of the various bar associations. I do not see why we should wait for them to make recommendations for the appointment of judges, practically taking that matter out of the hands of the Attorney General. I say further that at least some people in Canada believe in the election of judges. I am not prepared to go that far at the present time, though I can say that at times there is dissatisfaction on the part of bar associations and some of our local people about bringing judges into the county court of York from all over Ontario. We had three judges in that city who did all the work: the late Judge Coatsworth, then the late Judge Winchester; Judge Morson, and Judge Morgan. They were worked to death. Those judges were appointed from our own city.
What are the duties of county judges? Well, they have to do work in connection with the voters' list and in connection with many other municipal acts. These matters are referred to them for consideration. In my opinion they should have special knowledge of the localities in which they preside in civil and criminal cases. In this connection I do not agree with an argument used by a former minister. To a great extent they are judges handling municipal matters, under municipal laws and laws relating to the provinces under section 92 of the British North America Act. It is true that they take some cases which are under section 91. I believe the time has come however when some revision of policy should be made. There is criticism of the absence from this bill of penalties to check fatalities and accidents arising from motor cars, level crossings, drowning, fire hazards, fires in homes when parents are not present, and conditions of that kind. It is high time we in the House of Commons did something to remedy this condition by more modem legislation.
I believe that judges have for a long time earned larger salaries. We will remember that at one time a bill was introduced to exempt them from income tax. The first legislation of that kind was introduced by the late administration. Following the debate they were included under the income tax provisions. This is the highest court in Canada, the high court of parliament. Representations
are made from time to time by certain members of the bar. Only last Saturday an article appeared in a local paper with respect to the able hon. member for Calgary West. We must remember that we sit in the high court of parliament, and must protect the judiciary. Many members of the bar have earned salaries far greater than they have been paid as judges, and it pleases me to see some progress made in this connection.
The quicker a royal commission is appointed to revise the criminal code, the better. As chairman, I would suggest a great trial judge like Mr. Justice Keiller Mackay. There are many other competent judges, and have been many in the past. I have in mind the late chief justice W. R. Meredith, and a brother, Chief Justice R. M. Meredith, one of our most able judges. Both served on a commission to revise the statutes.
The public should receive more consideration than it does to-day. We must consider the onerous work performed by the Minister of Justice. I can tell him that unless he does less work and has more leisure, and devotes less time to his duties of office I fear for his state of health, remembering what happened to three of his predecessors. While he has given some of his work to. the new Solicitor General, a * competent man in his own right, I believe the only solution is a standing national legal committee, such as may be found in all the provinces, to consider all legal bills we have in this house. If we had a legal committee we would not be forced to operate in compliance with the rules of house procedure. Two special committees have met. We must keep in mind that this high court of parliament is the highest court in the land. Let us first attend to our own rules, and make a complete revision. In the disposition of civil and criminal cases in the courts we need a British North America Act for the living, not one for the dead. The rules of procedure for this chamber are obsolete. Let us put our own house in order first; let us recover the rights, functions and privileges we had in this chamber years ago. We do not want generosity. We are sent here by the high court of public opinion, the people of Canada, to do our duty properly and to the best of our ability.
As I read the text of the bill presented the other day I war reminded of the time when Charles I walked in the door of the House of Commons, and sat in the Speaker's chair. He was looking for five men, and approached Mr. Speaker Lenthall in the matter. Mr. Speaker Lenthall said: "May it please Your Majesty, I have neither eyes to see nor tongue to speak in this place but as the
Judges Act

house is pleased to direct me, whose servant I am here." The presiding officer in this chamber is the servant of the House of Commons, as is a judge or a chief justice in a court of law who under sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act represents parliament in civil and criminal cases.
Charity should begin at home. If we want to set an example for our law courts, and have a popular administration of justice, then let us set our own house in order. The first step would be to have a committee to revise the rules, so that we would have modern rules in this court of law, this highest court in the Dominion of Canada.

speechtext:
With much of what was said by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre I am sure all hon. members will be in agreement. He has asked why we should think of increasing the salaries of judges when old age pensioners are not getting enough to live on. Upon reflection however I believe he will realize that his main point is not well taken. In Canada, as in all British countries, one of the things in which we take greatest pride is our judiciary. Fundamental to the well-being of every nation is a respect for law and constituted authority. So far as a respect for law and authority is concerned I believe Canadians, perhaps more than those of any other nation, have reason to be proud. I fear however that within the last five or ten years there has been in our country a diminishing of that attitude. This is most regrettable.
I do not believe the Canadian citizen of today is as anxious to maintain the respect and obedience for the dignity of law as he was ten years ago.
When discussing salaries of judges I believe we should reflect upon the general attitude of the average Canadian toward Canadian laws and institutions. For the last ten or fifteen years, and perhaps for longer than that,
I think parliament has not properly appreciated the particular advantages accruing to Canadian citizenship from a strong and highly respected and dignified judiciary. To a great extent I believe parliament and legislators generally have lost perspective through the appointment of so many commissions and commissioners with powers to interpret and to decide law.
A survey of the duties of judges in our Canadian courts would disclose that they have very little leeway in rendering their judgments because they must follow legal precedent. They must follow a code of interpretation and administration of law which has been established for generations and is binding upon them. They must obey the judgments of superior courts, and in their decisions follow those superior court judgments. A good judge must

also take into consideration changing law to suit changing conditions. To guide him in this he has a mass of precedent from the court of record to which he belongs. This is not so of commissions or committees. During the war we watched the operations of a rental administrator, a man appointed to deal with problems affecting real property. Very often administrators of this type who are given power to interpret the law have never actually studied any law outside that which they are empowered to interpret. They have had no experience in administration of the law, and no precedents to follow. A judgment given to-day in a similar set of circumstances could be entirely opposite from one given to-morrow. There seems to be no way of checking this process, and the result does not add either to efficiency or to respect for law.
As to the matter of raising the salaries of judges, I have no doubt that each hon. member could think of a judge here and there who may not have a busy time of it and who, we may feel, is receiving adequate compensation for the work he is doing. But we can also think of many other judges who are doing much more work than they are being paid for. The hon. member for Broadview has referred to the judges of the county court of the county of York. The hon. member has indicated that they receive a salary of $6,000 a year. How does that compare with the salary of $15,000 received by the chairman of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation? Compare the ridiculous salaries of some civil servants appointed by this government with the salaries of the supreme court judges in Ontario, who when they are on itinerary seldom are able to spend more than a weekend at home. Then look at the death toll among the supreme court judges of Ontario through overwork in the last fifteen or twenty years, and we shall begin to realize that the public, instead of having gained a few paltry dollars by keeping the salaries and the number of the judges down, have really lost through not having enough judges to do the work and by not giving the increased number more work to do.
If we do increase the salaries of the county court judges-and I am not objecting to that -some of them will be getting more salary than the work they have to do entitles them to, but for the most part they will fully earn their salaries. I feel that parliament must in the very near future adopt a different policy in relation to our judges. Our judges are as independent as they can be. I think every Canadian will agree that the independence of our judges is one of the strongest attributes of our national life. Compare with some other officers, a judge who by experience is fitted to administer the law. Parliament passed a law

Judges Act
on income tax and appointed a commissioner of income tax. The commissioner of income tax and his officials give a ruling, we will say, that I do not like and which I think is against the law. If I appeal from his ruling I have to appeal to the very man who has given that ruling. I am not saying anything against the commissioner of income tax, but I say that he has been administering the policy laid down by the government and has grown up in the spirit of income taxation. When there is an appeal from his ruling he has no court to which he can go for legal precedents and direction, nor has he that breadth of view of public problems to deal with them in the light of various circumstances.
I think we should approach this question first from the point of view of a strong realization of the dignity and authority of our courts, and, secondly, with the realization that that authority is not any greater than it was in the past, if as great. Personally I do not believe Sts authority is as great as it was ten years ago. I believe that the people of Canada, who have been subject during the war years to a multitude of regulations and restrictions, have through their lack of knowledge of the law and perhaps from a desire to beat the law, acquired an unhealthy disrespect for the law. I believe that those who administer the law have the responsibility of returning the people to a greater respect for the law.
Look at 'the experience that a county court .judge has had. He has first of all had experience as a lawyer, whether that counts or not. Then when he sits on the county court bench he administers not only federal statutes, orders in council and regulations, but provincial law, orders in council and regulations, and municipal law and regulations, and he performs many other functions, all of which together give him a wealth of experience in interpreting the law.
In the provinces we have a municipal board administering municipal law. They are not members of the judiciary, and have not had the legal experience that our judicial officers have. The workmen's compensation board is another example, and if we want to take a federal example there is the wartime prices and trade board in almost every branch of which there are people engaged in interpreting a law for the enactment of which they themselves were responsible. A fundamental principle of British justice is that there shall be a differentiation between the judge, the prosecuting attorney, the jury, the witnesses, the plaintiff and the defendant, and we should bear that in mind. We should make sure that those who are appointed to office are able to perform the functions thereof.
Therefore in supporting to a degree the Minister of Justice in raising the salaries of the judges, I do so not because I believe that at the present time under our present policy they all require an increase, but because I feel that the time has come when we must and should see that o-ur judges are compensated for the increased work we shall be obliged to call upon them to do. But I would urge the Minister of Justice to take note also of the many officers who are performing judicial functions for which they have not judicial qualifications. If we are to increase the salaries of the county court judges, let us increase their work so that the people of Canada will also get the benefit of this increase.

Mr. Chairman, I seldom enter into a discussion of bills of this kind, for the reason that I am not a lawyer and the legal fraternity are well able to take care of them. But I desire to direct a question to the Minister of Justice which deals with the judiciary of my province, Prince Edward Island. The matter I shall mention I have often heard our lawyers discuss in Charlottetown and in different parts of the island.
In Prince Edward Island, the supreme court of which consists of three judges as at present constituted, we have no real court of appeal. I understand that when a judgment is given by one judge an appeal may be heard only by the remaining two judges of (the supreme court bench, with the result that if they disagree, as often happens, the trial judgment stands, even when the appeal judges disagree on points not even raised before these trial judges. I might also mention that the outcome of many cases is often unsatisfactory because the amount involved does not permit of an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. Does the bill now before us take care of such a situation as this, and has any consideration been given to the rearrangement of the judiciary of Prince Edward Island so as to provide for an efficient appeal court without adding to the existing number of judges?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: This bill does not take care of the situation referred to by the hon. member. Consideration has been given to it at various times ever since I assumed the office of Minister of Justice. One of the suggestions made was that the number of county court or district court judges be reduced and the number of high court judges increased so that there would always be three high court judges who had not participated in the judgment from which an appeal was taken. That has been discussed with the provincial authorities. The hon. member will realize that it is a matter within their juris-
Judges Act

diction. They are the ones who determine what courts they will have and how many judges constitute the bench of each court. Of course we have something to say in the matter. We do not admit that they can provide for any number of judges, a number that would be out of all proportion to the number required to handle the judicial business. But we try to meet the desires of the provincial authorities in providing sufficient judges for the courts which they organize as being the ones required for their local needs.
The suggestion of having one more high court judge and one less county court judge is one that has not been abandoned. It has not yet been accepted. It is a matter about which I understand the local authorities would like to get acceptance by the population of the counties. It may well be that it would require having the county court judges given jurisdiction over the whole island and not over just one district, because I do not think any one county would wish to abandon its rights to a judge in favour of the other counties. It is a matter which is still under consideration, I understand, by the local authorities of the province. The suggestion would involve some additional expense, but the local authorities have been told that I would undertake to recommend to parliament the additional expense that would be involved in the difference between the salary of a county court judge and a high court judge. It is something which the people of Prince Edward Island will have to make up their minds about. I do not think the hon. member would suggest that there be one judge added; I think he would agree that there are enough judges in Prince Edward Island to take care of all the judicial work, which arises there. It is a matter for the people of the province to determine how they want that judicial talent used to the best advantage.

I am sorry I cannot be as eloquent as the member for Cariboo, but I have a few observations to make on this bill and several suggestions to offer with regard to our Canadian judicial system. First, I would say that there has been some little question in this house in the past over travelling and subsistence allowance given judges serving on various commissions appointed by the government. A reference has been made to at least one case where a judge received an allowance sufficiently large to provide, for his wife while he was serving away from his judicial district. The government should have a clear-cut policy with regard to these cases, certainly so far as expense allowances are concerned. The fact that one judge receives special consideration, and the public is made aware of the situation, results in the public sometimes questioning whether judges are free from political favouritism on the part of the government. The judges are not to blame for that. I am not suggesting that they are, but I do suggest that the government is to blame for allowing it to happen. The house should insist that a flat rate be allowed for expenses and allowances for a judge's wife when away from home, and no deviation from that rate should be permitted. The judiciary should never be placed in such a position that the public may question its integrity.
Secondly, an impression prevails throughout the country that judges serving on commissions receive extra remuneration for such services, despite the fact that it has been stated in this house by the minister that only travelling and subsistence allowances have been allowed in addition to the salary normally received by the judge in the position he holds. I believe it is timely now to make
Judges Act

a statement to the public that that is not so, and that the rule has not been broken with regard to the payment of any judges serving on commissions, so that the public in general may be made aware of the true state of things.
Thirdly, I question the method of appointing judges which has been in vogue in Canada ever since the passing of the British North America Act. When a Liberal government is in power Liberal judges are appointed-that is, Liberal in political faith-and should a Conservative government take office at the next election I should not be surprised to see judges of another political stripe appointed, namely, Conservatives. It is obvious that these appointments are political. Too often the appointments are a reward for political activities. Not infrequently, appointments are made to take care of some old war horse who has outlived his usefulness to the party. On the whole, I believe that the men appointed, either by this government ' or by previous governments, have been good men. I am not suggesting anything to the contrary. I am not suggesting that any of the men in the past have been incompetent. I say, however, that political appointees generally must find it a little difficult to bury the hatchet once they are made judges. They are human, and if they have been in political life for some considerable time they must retain some little political prejudice. While, mind you, there has been very little evidence that that is so, we hear rumours unfortunately from time to time that it is. I believe a better system could be devised than the one we have, and I would suggest that when the appointment of a judge is found necessary, 'recommendations for the position be invited from the law society of the province in which the judge is to be appointed.

We find this situation developing. The young enterprising lawyer gets into political life. I have had experience in this particular field; I know what happened in one instance, where in a partnership one lawyer was a Conservative and the other a Liberal. They were not going to overlook their opportunities. I suppose if a third member was required in the partnership he would be a C.C.F. member. It could happen. If that were done then they would be always on the right side for any appointment that was being made; one or the other of the group would be selected.
If my suggestion with regard to appointments to the bench should be followed-I know it would not be popular-it would tend to safeguard the public against politics playing a part in the administration of justice.
I would further suggest that some method of promotion be evolved for judges. This suggestion may be a little more popular than the previous one. Every hon. member has observed the appointment of lawyers to high judicial places, even to the supreme court, I am told, without any experience whatever on the bench. I believe that is wrong; I think the principle is wrong. It is my opinion, and only my opinion, that judges should be appointed first to a district court, or to the county court, as it is called in Ontario, or to courts of equivalent status. The experience gained in that court would prepare a judge for work in a higher court. The next step upward would be to the court of king's bench. He would receive that appointment provided he had done acceptable work in the court to which he had been previously appointed. Then judges of the appeal court could be selected from the court of king's bench. I do
not think it is sound to select men who have had no judicial training whatever and appoint them to high court positions.
The bill before us deals mainly with increases in judges' salaries and allowances for federal judges. It will involve considerable controversy; it will involve a considerable increase in public expenditure. I find myself definitely opposed to such a large increase at this time. Judges can still be found who will gladly serve for S5,000 a year, together with the. other allowances which they receive, consisting chiefly of travelling and sustenance allowances when they are away from home. That is a fairly substantial salary, and as I have pointed out before, there always seem to be many men who want the appointments. That is proof in itself that they are adequately paid.
Some of our judges are not too busy. I have in mind a certain district court judge in Saskatchewan who had no more than twelve cases a year. In addition to his work on the bench he has the administration of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, which involves some extra work. But he is not a busy man. You can always tell how busy people are by what they do with their spare time.
I suggested a moment ago that $5,000 seemed to be a fairly substantial salary, but most of our judges in Saskatchewan-and I think this holds good throughout the dominion-receive an additional salary as judges of the surrogate court. That additional salary usually amounts to $1,000, and is added to the $5,000 which they receive as district or county judges. I believe I am right in that.

Mr. Chairman, I have rather full notes here on this subject, but I must confess that if I did not know the hon. member for Weyburn to be very honest and capable I would almost think that somehow or other he had stolen my notes, for what I am going to say is almost identical with what he had in mind; and of course as a result I need not take up a great deal of the time of the committee.
There is a point, however, I should like to make here in respect to the argument that the salaries of these judges are so high that there is a tremendous spread between their incomes and the incomes of thousands of people in our country who get so little; and the old age pensioners have been referred to in this respect. This is true, and we have no argument against it except that fundamentally we are arguing at cross purposes. The fundamental error is not that one is getting so much and the other is getting so little; the fundamental error is that under our present system of tax finance, when we raise the salaries of judges or
fMr. McKay.]
government appointees we are spending somebody else's money, and that is where the rub comes.
When these matters are under discussion here I cannot help thinking that there are two attitudes that may be taken. One seems to be the attitude taken by all the parties except the Social Credit party; the other is the attitude taken by us. The one attitude is that there is only so much money to go round, and that money must come from the taxpayers. Just so long as you agree that is so, then so long shall we have the argument that there is unfair distribution of the scarcity of money; and on that basis the argument would be sound. But the Social Credit philosophy in that respect is a philosophy of spending. That may sound strange to some who have not heard of it before, but money is only good in so far as you are able to spend it. For that reason we believe our taxation system can be extensively revised, even to a point of almost doing away with it, apart from some injustices that might occur; and that if only we can look at this matter as being the spending of new money which is not other people's money, perhaps that problem would dissolve. Of course the argument that increasing the salaries of judges is an injustice imposed upon those getting lower salaries would have been a good argument to advance when our own indemnities were increased by reason of a 12,000 expense allowance. We did not hear those arguments then. My observation, of course, is that we knew we needed it and could not get along without it; nevertheless the same argument applies.	,
It has always struck me as rather strange that those who administer the law get more than those who make it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

That is so, too. I do not want any unfair inference to be taken from my remarks. I am quite satisfied now with the indemnity and allowance we are getting, and I am well aware of the fact that those who administer the law must have a background of training which costs a great deal of money. They have to go to university; they have to be articled to some law firm; they have to start out in business; they take a chance on whether or not their ability will get them somewhere, and I know all these things have to be taken into consideration. But regardless of the remuneration paid those who make the law, let us take as an illustration the one person in this country who after all is responsible for the administration of all the legal aspects involved in the country's business. I refer to

the Minister of Justice. I believe his salary is $10,000, with perhaps an allowance. But I am certain he has a tremendous responsibility. These judges get higher salaries than he receives. I could mention others. Take the Prime Minister, who gets a certain salary. I would have to turn to my estimates to refresh my memory as to the exact figure, but it occurs to me that the Prime Minister does not get as much as the chief justice of Canada, and he gets no pension when he is defeated at the next, election. Then there are other government appointees who receive more than the Prime Minister receives. We have the Minister of Finance being paid $10,000 a year, and the governor of the Bank of Canada receiving $30,000 a year. I could never quite understand how that came about.
I shall refer to one other matter, to which I believe I shall not do 'better justice than did the hon. member for Weybum, when he referred to the manner of appointing judges. To many who become judges the appointments are just juicy political plums. I refer to the matter in that way because I am certain that the appointment of judges is not necessarily based upon the ability of the appointees as lawyers. Many who receive appointments to the bench h'ave not had outstanding careers in law. There are men who have outstanding legal careers and who have divorced themselves from politics but who, in my opinion, do not stand a ghost of a chance of becoming judges in Canada. I believe therefore that some other method should be devised for the appointment of judges.
I shall take my seat after asking a question. Are the salaries of judges subject to income tax, and are their expense accounts as outlined in the bill subject to income tax?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Salaries of judges are subject to income tax. Travelling allowances provided are not taxed.

I have listened with interest to the discussion which has taken place this morning, and would suggest a medium through which we could raise the salaries of judges without adding any greater expense to the country. I believe we have too many judges. Reference has been made to the large amount of work they are doing-and this may be so in some cases. However I can, visualize many counties in the rural sections of Canada where the judges could easily take on the duties of one or two more counties, and still do justice to their work. I believe that probably we would attract a better class of judges if we paid higher salaries, and I would favour such an increase in salaries. At the same time I believe there should be a reduction in the number of judges.
I hear a good deal of criticism from the fact that judges withhold too long decisions in cases they have tried. It appears that there should be some provision whereby in a reasonable length of time a judge would be compelled to give a decision in a case. The expenses in connection with the trials of many of these cases have been heavy, and yet there does not appear to be any way of compelling the judge to give his decision. I believe it would be in the public interest if action were taken along this line.
Speaking generally I believe the work of the judiciary in Canada has been satisfactory, and that we should see to it that they receive a remuneration which would make them independent and fit them to do a better job in the administration of our laws.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING JUDGES OP DOMINION AND PROVINCIAL COURTS
speechtext:
As a rule I am not in favour of increasing public expenditures, but in this instance I am heartily in favour of the move made by the Minister of Justice. For too long have the judges who administer our laws been underpaid. I welcome this opportunity to support the action, of the Minister of Justice in bringing this bill forward.
Some novel suggestions have been heard in committee this morning. The hon. member for Cariboo referred to Solomon. Well, judging from the number he had: around his house, Solomon was probably a better judge of women than of most other things. And as to Daniel, he would probably have qualified as a judge at a circus, because he landed in the lions' den.
The suggestion that non-lawyers should be appointed as judges in our courts is a novel one. I do not suppose that even a socialist would set a blacksmith to lay bricks on a house. After all, any man holding a responsible position must have some training for the position he occupies. Judges have to have a practice in law at the bar for a term of years before they become qualified to hold judicial posts.
The hon. member for Cariboo referred to the administration of law by juries. Sometimes juries are right and sometimes they are wrong. I am not going to say in which class most of their findings would fall. But as a solicitor who has been practising for a good many years I have often wondered what particular use there was for juries in a country where we have such well-trained judges on the bench. Some of the findings of juries upon facts given in evidence make one wonder how those findings were arrived at. Let me add, however, that where juries are employed they are given direction by a judge who, after all, presides in the court and has control of its proceedings. It seems to me hon. members
Judges Act

are going a long way when they advocate a system, such as was suggested this morning, under which we would not have trained lawyers on the bench to administer matters coming before them.
As usual the hon. member for Macleod had to give us the social credit theory-and I understood it this morning just as well as I have understood all the social credit theories we have listened to. I sit opposite them, and hear them all the time. Never yet, however, have I had the satisfaction of coming to a final conclusion of what it is all about, beyond the fact that it adds to the volume of Hansard and to the satisfaction of hon. members who have spoken.

speechtext: Keep your mind open; you will learn.

The hon. member for Macleod also referred to juicy political plums. Let me tell him that there are many practising barristers and solicitors who do not look upon these appointments as juicy plums. Many of our best lawyers refuse to take appointments to the bench-and the Minister of Justice knows it. The result is that we must take men who have not the Outstanding qualifications possessed by many others in the profession. For these reasons I certainly do not look upon an appointment to the bench as a juicy political plum.
Reference was made this morning to the law societies of the different provinces. For fifteen years I have been a bencher of the Law Society of Upper Canada. I am now a life member of that body, and I know that very often this matter has been discussed by it. They are actively interested in having the very best appointments to the bench.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose on Thursday last I was discussing the question of dominion-provincial relations. Before I proceed with my remarks to-day I propose to take a few minutes of the time of the house to summarize briefly what I had to say up to that time.
I had shown that the question of dominion-provincial relations had first been set out in [DOT]the British North America Act of seventy-nine years ago; that that act set up a federal system in Canada, and not a unitary system-in other words a two-government system, not a one-government system-with a central government on the one hand and provincial governments on the other.
I had pointed out that this federal system placed responsibilities on each of these two types of government, and on one of them, namely the provincial governments, it had placed a limitation of taxing powers, the provinces being confined to direct taxation and denied indirect taxation. I had shown that the advantages arising from confederation had not been equally distributed as between the different sections of Canada, not because of any deliberate intention, but partly because of the accident of the degree of centralization that it brought about.
I had shown that certain national policies, particularly the tariff, had borne inequitably on different sections of the nation. I had shown that certain social services and the cost of those services, responsibilities largely of the provinces, had multiplied rapidly in the seventy-nine years, and that as a result, certain areas in Canada either had a very low standard of social services or had them only by imposing such a high rate of taxation as to be almost confiscatory.
I had shown as well that in the seventy-nine years since confederation there had been several adjustments between the dominion and and the provinces with respect to subsidies and so on, most of them, as we see them today, more or less minor in character. But in the nineteen thirties the situation had become desperate, and in 1937 this government appointed a royal commission to deal with the matter. That commission after three years' work had reported in 1940. The report failed to secure the agreement of the province in 1941; and then the government, realizing that something had to be done and practically everybody accepting that decision, entered into the wartime tax suspension agreements with the provinces, whereby the provinces vacated certain tax fields and the government

The Budget-Mr. Bracken
reimbursed the provinces to the extent substantially of the revenues which they had been receiving from those taxes.
With the termination of the war and the wartime tax suspension agreements being due to terminate, some next fall and others next spring, the federal government came forward with its August 1945 dominion-provincial proposals. Those proposals dealt not only with finance and taxation but with an expanded programme of social security and with a programme of public investment. Those proposals were modified slightly again in January of this year; and then in May of this year, in a conference with the provinces, failure to secure agreement was again the result. On June 27 last, when the Minister of Finance brought in his budget, he brought forward a much watered-down proposal which has been advanced to the provinces one by one since that time.
I had shown that in these various approaches to the problem there had been a progressive increase in the tax burden proposed to be levied on the Canadian people in order to meet this problem, increasing from $40,000,000 in ,1940 under the proposals of the Rowell-Sirois commission's report to over $80,000,000 under the wartime tax suspension agreements, and to approximately $180,000,000 under the first proposals of the dominion government advanced last August, and approximately $200,000,000 in its modified proposals of last January; to which had to be added large sums for social security and public investment, bringing the tax burden sooner or later to be imposed on the Canadian people to $600,000,000 in the case of the dominion government and an addition of $200,000,000 on the provinces or a total of some $800,000,000 in all.
At the hour of adjournment on Thursday last I was dealing with the government's excuse for its meagre programme of tax reductions for this year, and for its action in omitting from its present programme the social security and public investment aspects of the proposals which it advanced last August. The efforts of the government in trying to represent that tax reductions by the government were dependent upon the approval of its proposals by the provinces I suggest, Mr. Speaker, leaves a false impression which is unworthy of the government of Canada. The government had to reduce taxation under the wartime tax suspension agreements of 1942 with the provinces. In its agreements with the nine provinces it was required by the provinces to get out of those tax fields to some extent at the end of the war. I know something about it, because I was on the other end of the agreement with
Manitoba at that time. The provinces would not have gone into the agreements if they had not felt that they would be terminated when the war was over and that they could get back into their vacated tax fields without an undue burden on their taxpayers. In that connection I might read one section from the tax suspension agreement of the dominion with the province of Manitoba. I do not know whether the clause reads exactly the same in the agreements with the other provinces, but I presume it does. This is how section 20 of the tax suspension agreement with Manitoba reads:
The dominion shall have the sole right to levy taxes on personal and corporation incomes of the calendar year ending on the thirty-first day of December nearest to the date of the termination of this agreement, and with respect to personal and corporation incomes in the following calendar year undertakes to reduce its rates of taxes by such an amount as will enable the province again to use the income tax and corporation tax fields, and in particular the dominion undertakes to reduce its rates of tax on corporation incomes by at least 10 per cent of such incomes.
That was a definite undertaking in the agreement signed four years ago. In compliance with that undertaking the government had no choice but to make these minor reductions in taxation which the minister announced in his budget.
Now with respect to the abandonment by the government of its social security programme and the public investment programme, what explanation does the government give for abandoning these two features of its 1945 proposal to the provinces? It is going ahead now province by province with the possibility of less than nine agreements being made; possibly eight, possibly seven, possibly six, possibly less; no man knows-possibly all. One cannot but regret this plan of approaching the provinces one at a time. One is compelled to wonder if the dominion is really anxious to have the larger provinces come in. I suspect it would rather see the larger provinces stay out.
The dominion is now paying $88 million to the provinces under the wartime tax suspension agreements. This amount will be saved the dominion treasury as the agreements expire, and if a province does not enter into a new agreement the dominion saves the rental it would otherwise have to pay. The government therefore has no right to say it has to abandon its social security and public investment policies because it has not been able to get the agreement of the provinces. If the government reaches agreement with all the provinces, it will pay what it has agreed
The Budget-Mr. Bracken

to pay-$198 million, it is estimated, for the year 1947; and if it makes agreements with less than nine provinces the cost to the government will be less. So why talk about abandoning the social security and public investment features of this policy which it proclaimed so loudly last August? In comparison with the August 1945 proposals as amended by them in January, the saving to the dominion under the government's present plan would be colossal. All this present plan can' cost the government of Canada is $198 million a year; the last-year plan might cost and would in due course cost the Canadian people, dominion and provincial-and they are the same people-$800 million a year. As I said, in comparison with the August 1945 proposals subsequently amended, the lessened cost to the dominion under the government's present plan would be colossal. For that reason I say that the dominion government's attempt to saddle upon the non-agreeing provinces the responsibility for postponement of their social security programme is just pure bluff.
But the government will say that unless it has the exclusive use of these three fields of taxation, income, corporation and succession duties, it will not know what the provinces are going to do in them. The government hints that while it may be endeavouring to raise national production and national income, the provinces in the meantime may be trying to lower it. This is another type of superiority complex which is unworthy of the dominion. The dominion government says it wants to pursue anti-depression policies; is it to be assumed that the provinces will want to pursue pro-depression policies? This superior attitude which the dominion is developing towards the provinces is anything but conducive to good dominion-provincial relations. Is the dominion government assuming that if it reduces its corporation and personal income tax rates by small amounts to raise the level of production and employment, the province of Ontario or of Quebec or of British Columbia is going to be so stupid or so reckless of its own interests and the interests of Canada that it will penalize individuals and industries by imposing higher taxes? The logic of the government's argument is that the provinces can no longer be trusted to act responsibly in fiscal matters. It brings into the open in a way that has never been brought out before this superior attitude of the dominion government and its secret invisible government of advisers.	[DOT]
A few centuries ago kings and ministers fell into the hands of alchemists, those who claimed they could produce gold from the philosopher's stone. Gold has not the import-
ance to-day that it had a few centuries ago; but we are building up in Ottawa with the concurrence of this government, a public service which is beguiling the people into believing that there is some magic or mysterious way which is open to dominion officials, but to no others, to provide services and goods without imposing great obligations by way of taxation. If the present government's social security and public investment policies were sound last August and sound until last April, then they were also sound in June, when the government brought in its present proposals. The dominion has no justification for dropping its social security programme because of any action taken by the provinces. All the facts indicate, Mr. Speaker, that the government fears to proceed with its own policies, that it fears the consequences of the heavy burden of taxation they would impose. It looks as if the government was pleased when the conference failed, particularly if it could lay the blame on somebody else.
Let me summarize briefly my views with respect to this matter. My observations of the last nine years, during which I happen to have been very close to this problem, indicate to me two things. First, the people of Canada will not be satisfied without an agreement; second, they will not be satisfied without an agreement arrived at by conference with all the provinces as opposed to one made by the government's piecemeal procedure.
My recommendations in this matter can be stated very briefly. They are just four in number.
First the dominion government should repeal certain minor taxes, such as the gasoline tax, amounting to three cents per gallon, and the tax on electricity of eight per cent of the consumers' bills, which taxation fields it invaded as a wartime measure. To comment on that in passing, let me remind the house that in the case of this gasoline tax, three cents per gallon, farmers have been held down with respect to farm prices even as their costs are rising; and now the dominion continues to impose three cents a gallon tax not only on gasoline used by farmers but also on gasoline used by fishermen and many others. With respect to the eight per cent tax on consumers' bills for electricity, I know of two provinces, Ontario and Manitoba-there may be others-the governments of which are taxing their whole people, in order to do what? To lessen the cost by fifty per cent of the distribution of electrical energy to outlying communities. In the face of that generous policy the dominion government comes along and puts on an eight per cent consumer's tax on electricity, offsetting to at least that degree

The Budget-Mr. Bracken
the policies of getting electrical energy extended to outlying areas. That is number one.
My second recommendation is that the dominion should stay out of these minor tax fields and leave them to the provinces. I cannot take time to-day to enlarge upon these things, but let me just say that in 1867 the provinces were required to give up their revenues in the form of indirect taxes, the chief source of revenue they had; and now, seventy-nine years later, they are asked to give up their important sources of direct taxation- income, corporation and succession duties; and the dominion still wants to stay in the other and minor fields of direct taxation. I say that the dominion should stay out of the minor fields and leave them to the provinces.
Third, the dominion should call another conference in order to try to achieve a united front in the attack on post-war problems.
Fourth, there should be set up in this dominion a central dominion-provincial committee to study dominion-provincial relations so that the present situation may be improved. In any event we should have a studied and acceptable plan for the time when the government's present five-year tax agreement plans either fail or come to an end. This question of dominion-provincial relations in Canada is too important not to have the best brains study it for as long as may be necessary in order to arrive at a plan that will receive the practically unanimous support of the Canadian people.
Briefly those are my suggestions. As for leaving these minor tax fields to the provinces, I wish to bring not only my own humble judgment but the judgment of the Rowell-Sirois commission, set up in 1937, which made a better study of this question than any other body that 'has studied it since confederation. What was proposed by that commission was that the dominion should have the sole recourse to income, corporation and succession duties; but that commission left no doubt in the minds of the Canadian people where it stood in respect of the other minor taxation fields. This is what the commission had to say at page 85 of volume 2 of its report: Each province will be left with, relatively speaking, a remarkably stable revenue. A large part of the revenue of some will consist of a fixed cash payment from the dominion. The taxes with highly variable yields will have been transferred to the dominion. Those with fairly constant yields will remain. (The chief exceptions are the public domain revenues and the mining tax rebate in some provinces, and the profits from the sale of liquor.)
Listen to this-the report continues:
It is implicit in the plan, but should be clearly stated, that the dominion will respect the tax fields left to the provinces. Adjustments in the joint domininn-provineial-municipal tax structure will undoubtedly be necessary and desirable from time to time, but the dominion can no longer consider itself a free and independent agent to take unilateral action to this end when it pleases. The essence of the plan is to leave provinces and municipalities with adequate, suitable revenues, and this would clearly be defeated if the dominion should extend its taxation into fields already occupied by the provinces or on objects jointly taxed without making satisfactory compensatory adjustments. Such action would violate the whole spirit of the arrangement.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the view of the dominion's own commission after three years of study. It is the commission's view with respect to the attitude of the dominion government towards the minor fields of direct taxation in which the dominion now persists in remaining, even though it is asking the governments to give up the three large fields of taxation.
In addition to the views expressed by the Rowell-Sirois commission, I might point to the views of one of the provincial premiers, the premier of Nova Scotia. What he had to say may be read at the bottom of page 38, and on to page 39 of the proceedings of April 29 of the dominion-provincial conference. The date, as I say, is April 29, 1946, and I should like to read what he had to say about this particular aspect of the problem:
How do the provinces stand under the proposals? We have two exclusive fields of taxation, one of which fields is valueless. There is joint occupancy of other small fields such as gasoline, amusements, electricity and the like. Then there are the proposed grants, which the dominion calculated at $15 per head, increasing as the production of this country increases. In return we are asked to surrender our rights to collect income and corporation taxes, two fields which, as I said, yielded last year something in excess of one and a half billion dollars. We have then to surrender the rights to collect income and corporation tax, two fields which I stated last year yielded something over one and a half billion dollars. That is the position which the provinces are asked to take.
Let me ask you, Mr. Chairman, and the delegates here, whether they represent the dominion or the provinces, let me ask anyone who is within sound of my voice, let me ask that great body to which we as public servants are all accountable, the citizens of our provinces or of Canada, let me ask any of those people whether they think that is a fair or honourable or dignified position in which to place the. provinces in this dominion? Provincial autonomy will be gone. Provincial independence will vanish. Provincial dignity will disappear. Provincial governments will become mere annuitants of Ottawa. Provincial public life-and I do not think these words are too strong-will be debased and degraded. I cannot think that such a state of affairs is desired by the representatives of the government of Canada here to-day, my one-time colleagues. I am sure that they have no wish or desire to see such a state of affairs come
The Budget-Mr. Bracken

to pass in this country nor can I believe that such a state of affairs is desired by the people of this country.
So much for the views of the Rowell-Sirois commission and of the premier of Nova Scotia.
As I said, at confederation the provinces gave up their indirect taxes, which then represented almost their total source of revenue. They gave them up for a subsidy payment which, even now, seventy-nine years later, amounts only to about $17,000,000; and now, after that seventy-nine years, the provinces are asked by the dominion to give up their chief sources of direct taxation-income and corporation and succession duties. When the provinces say, "At least leave us a few minor fields of taxation," the dominion says no. I suggest that such an attitude is not democratic. It is not cooperative. It represents not the conference mind but the dictatorial mind. It represents coercion. It smacks of centralized dictatorship. It represents the type of public discussion that this country ought, until the last extremity, to try to avoid.
I come now to the second of the two topics I indicated that I wished to deal with, namely, the question of the attitude of the government of Canada toward the cooperative movement. With respect to the cooperative movement let me at the outset make two brief comments. To me the cooperative movement is one of the counter balancing forces to the present trend in government toward centralization and bureaucratic controls. I regard the cooperative movement as a bulwark against both cartelization on the one hand and state socialism on the other. It is a movement that is here; it is a good movement, and nothing must be permitted which will hamper its development along sound lines.
My position with respect to the government's proposed taxation of cooperatives can be briefly stated in five sentences. Before I state these views let me say that any responsible government must try to find a system of taxation which is fair to all its constituents. Neither this government nor any other can let itself get into a position where unfair taxation laws drive people from one type of enterprise into another. Having said that, let me outline our position with respect to these cooperatives.
First, we are opposed to the government policy of imposing taxes on moneys which would have been paid out in patronage dividends by certain cooperatives in 1944 and 1945. We have a situation in Canada where, from 1930 until now, these organizations were not taxed on patronage dividends, or savings, or earnings, or whatever you choose to call them;

and the government now comes forward with a policy saying that after 1946 they are not to be so taxed, but with respect to what has gone before they say: We are going to put a tax on these earnings, or dividends, or what>
ever you call them, for the two years 1944 and 1945.

The law has not been changed in this respect since I do not know when. These organizations were not taxed and have not been taxed as yet. After all these years the government has come forward with a policy which says that from now on they should not be taxed but they are going to be made to pay for 1944 and 1945, the two best

The Budget-Mr. Bracken
years that they ever had. We are opposed to the government policy of imposing taxes on moneys which would have been paid out for patronage dividends by certain cooperative organizations in 1944 and 1945.
Second, we are opposed to the provision governing payment of patronage dividends, by which they must be paid in cash. We take the position that cooperatives should be allowed to pay these dividends either in cash or its equivalent of any kind.
Third, we are opposed to the government limitation that transfers of stock ownership cannot be made free of tax except on purchases made subsequent to the year 1941. I shall make some observations on these latter matters in a moment or two.
Fourth, we are opposed to the government's policy of compelling cooperatives to pay patronage dividends to non-members. We are opposed to this because it is a matter of internal cooperative management and something which should not be made the concern of the government. .

Fifth, with regard to the government's plan that taxes must be paid on three per cent of capital employed, I want a further explanation from the government when we go into committee. As the matter now stands this plan is capable of different interpretations, and in addition it is not made clear how in practice it will be administered.
Let me now deal more specifically with the government's belated policy of dealing with pool taxation over the years prior to 1946. Ordinarily a taxing authority is supposed to know its business. What would we think as individuals if the government had been in doubt for some sixteen years as to whether we were liable for taxes or not? Members of this government had let the pools remain untaxed from 1930 to 1941 without protest.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And the preceding government.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext: All right, if that helps the hon. member any.
