speechtext: It does.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Take your head out of the sand and look forward.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Then, under pressure from the pool's competitors the government felt obliged to say, "Well, we don't know; you may be taxable or you may not." This was before the election. They said: "We will try it out in the courts. Let us have a test case." And before the test case had reached the courts, the government said, "No; we will appoint a royal commission." That was also before an election. Now for the first time in sixteen years the government has a policy with respect to taxing cooperatives. Now they say to the pools: "If you will give us two cents of the 3i cents patronage dividends that would have been paid in 1944 and 1945 if doubts had not arisen in the mind of the government, we will call the matter off."
This government has asked the farmers of Canada-I will be a little more specific; this government has asked the wheat growers of Canada-to take $155 a bushel for a certain portion of their wheat and $1.55 a bushel for certain other portions, while the world price is at a vastly greater figure. The pool organizations supported that policy loyally, and as a recompense the government comes along and says that on the amount that you regard as patronage dividends in the last two years amounting to approximately 3i cents a bushel we will take two cents. That is the government plan, even though from now on it is going to discontinue it as a matter of considered government policy.
The government has been forcing western farmers to take $1.25 basis Fort William, plus a participation certificate, for a part of their wheat. It has been forcing them to sell on export markets at $1.55 a bushel, considerably below the price paid to their competitors. Let me put it this way. Suppose the government had made up its mind earlier, as it should have done; what would have been the result? The result would have been that the years 1944 and 1945 would have been treated precisely as the years 1946 and 1947 are to be treated from now on. The government could not possibly bring forward that kind of policy and say it is right to tax these people for two years and then it is wrong forever afterwards to tax them. The government either had a taxation policy or it had not. If it had not a taxation policy, it has no business now using its power to extract money from Canadian citizens under the threat of prolonged and costly litigation.
I want to deal for a moment or two with the restrictions with which the payment of patronage dividends are surrounded. As I read resolution No. 12 the government is going to require that patronage dividends be paid in cash. If the government persists in

The Budget-Mr. Bracken

very friendly with one of the commissioners who is now dead. We know, therefore, whose was Esau's hand and whose was Jacob's voice in 1941. But in 1946 it would be quite interesting to know whose was Jacob's voice, while Esau's hand was the same.
Times change. Time marches on. I am sure that if the Rowell-Sirois report has been implemented by the government, it is precisely due to the able speech delivered by the present leader of the opposition on that fateful day, January 14, 1941. The hon. member was then, as he is to-day, a man of great experience, the dean of the premiers of the nine provinces. Here is what he said about the Rowell-Sirois report:
This commission was required by its terms of reference to make a very wide inquiry. It has done this in a most thorough manner. In the judgment of many competent authorities, it is one of the most intensive and complete public inquiries ever undertaken in the British empire on the workings of a federal state. Canadians now, and in the days to come, may differ as to the wisdom or efficacy of the specific recommendations of the commissioners; but the careful and exhaustive research on which the recommendations were based will stand to-morrow, as it stands to-day, a bench-mark to which we shall always return.
Yes-"Canadians now, and in the days to come"; who would have said then that in the days to come it would be on this 23rd day of July that the hon. gentleman would deny what he was boasting with such emphasis five years ago?
But that is not all, Mr. Speaker. I quote again the same gentleman:
We in Manitoba-
Now it is "we in Ottawa"-there is a slight difference.
We in Manitoba-
It may be "we in Toronto"-
We in Manitoba respect this report because it comes from men whose ability and integrity are generally admitted-men who have had the advantage of the fullest possible facilities for reaching sound conclusions-facilities that have never before in Canadian history been provided to those charged with similar responsibilities. To the men responsible for this outstanding contribution to our national life, I wish on behalf of the people and the government of Manitoba to convey our most sincere congratulations and thanks.
An then as he sat at the clerk's table, the hon. member summarized, the four major recommendations of the commission. What were they?
1. The transfer to the dominion government of a wholly modern responsibility-unemployment relief.

When the war came along unemployment to a large extent decreased, and that question is not argued by the hon. member at this time. Then:
2.	A change in the method of arriving at dominion financial assistance to the provinces.
This is very important. It changed the basis of taxation according to the British North America Act. Now let us see what will please the premiers of the provinces:
3.	The transfer to the dominion government of the sole right to levy income tax, inheritance tax and corporation taxes.
And No. 4:
4.	The assumption by the dominion of the debts of the provinces.
The subtitles were these: Implementation of Substance of Report Essential to National Unity. Very important, Mr. Speaker. Another one was this:	Implementation of Report
Enhances Provincial Autonomy. Then under the subtitle, Unsoundness of Tax Structure Inherent in Constitution, I read this:
As long as the provinces have resort only to direct taxation, and their revenues are supplemented by the dominion only through subsidies calculated on the obsolete basis of population- just so long the dominion cannot impose the taxation which it should on incomes and inheritances without seriously reducing the important sources of revenue of many provinces, including certainly Manitoba. We suggest that as long as the provinces retain the field of direct taxation, our national tax structure will continue to present this irrational aspect.
Another subtitle, Mr. Speaker-most in-teresting-was this: Ill-Balanced Tax Structure Bears Heavily upon Low Income Consumers and Unprotected Producers, and under that heading I find this:
Let me touch on this for just a moment. As long as the dominion has to raise the bulk of its revenues by indirect taxes upon consumption which bear most heavily upon the low income groups, its taxes will continue to inflict the grave injustice which has been inflicted during the depression upon the poor, upon the consumer, and upon the farmer and other producers who are not protected by the tariff. The poorer a man, the larger his family, the less protected his market-the more heavily this tax structure bears upon him, regardless of the province in which he lives.
Some of the other subtitles are: Heavy Indirect Taxes Increase Cost of Living-Ill-Balanced Tax Structure Leaves Relatively Heavier Burden upon Low Income Groups- Present Tax Structure Transfers Income from Relatively Poor to Relatively Rich. Under the subtitle "Decision Provinces Must Make", I find this:
The decision which the provinces must make is whether they shall retain their right to impose these direct taxes and get less and less

The Budget-Mr. Pouliot
from them, or whether they shall voluntarily relinquish them now for adequate considerations, financial and otherwise.
That is what was said by the hon. leader of the opposition a little more than five years ago. I regret to have to remind him of what he said on that occasion. It may or may not be of some embarrassment to him, but as he is the one who by his eloquence was responsible for the adoption of the Rowell-Sirois report by the government, it is my duty to put this before the house so that even those who were not in public life at the time will not be unaware of the stand taken by the hon. gentleman on that occasion.
As I read the amendment which has been moved by the financial critic of the opposition I find that his first complaint is that the budget does not provide for tax reductions in the calendar year 1946. No tax reductions!
I am for tax reductions provided that the expenditure is not too heavy, and I will have i word to say about that in a moment.
When the Prime Minister sponsored the motion to establish the Rowell commission I thought that his purpose was to clear the skies, to relieve Canada of all the difficulties which had been a cause of contradictory jurisprudence, and to give ample opportunity to the government at Ottawa and to the provinces to stand up and be self-supporting for years to come.
If we read the British North America Act attentively and read at the same time what was said by Lord Carnarvon, who sponsored our constitution in the House of Lords, we shall realize that the purpose of those statesmen who had foresight and who did not change their minds every year or every five years, ivas to create independent entities, to create provinces that were to be independent of the dominion government and of the dominion parliament just as much as they were to be independent of each other. The word 'exclusively" is repeated time and time again to show that the jurisdiction of one authority is not the jurisdiction of the other. The speech of that great Englishman can be summarized in these words:	we will teach them,
teach Ottawa and the provinces, we will teach them all to mind their own business. It is precisely because of the encroachment that has been made upon these separate fields of jurisdiction, by the dominion on provincial ground and by the provinces on federal ground, that we reached the time when the commission was created.
And what happened? What was it? The intelligensia appeared before the commission from everywhere. They even brought Bruen-ing, the ex-Chancellor of Germany, to tell
the commission what had happened over there and what should happen here. I asked Mr. Dunning if Bruening had come as an expert, and he said, no, as a witness. Nevertheless he came to illuminate the minds of the commissioners. One of them was coach to the present leader of the opposition when he was premier of the province of Manitoba. All sorts of men came before the commission. And what was the purpose of the commission in drafting its report? The purpose was precisely to annihilate the provinces, and I am surprised that a clear-sighted man like the leader of the opposition did not realize that when he bestowed such praise on the commission. I remember, and I mentioned it in the house in February, 1941, that in January of that year on the eve of the meeting of the dominion-provincial conference at Ottawa I heard a professor from Queen's in one of his broadcasts saying:	We should not
have ten countries in Canada, ten small independent nations-and he had a word of contempt for the ten small countries-we should have only one big country.
I can tell the hon. gentleman that I am very glad that the government was a little cautious about implementing that report., because if one were to take for granted what he said on January 14, 1941, nothing would be left to the provinces; they would be completely destroyed; for they would have no powers of taxation. It is dangerous to listen to bad counsellors, bad advisers; and when I say that to the hon. gentleman who leads the opposition I mean it, and I make a great distinction between himself and the board of strategy of his intelligentsia in Toronto. I am sorry for him that he listens to them, that he is guided by them, that he becomes a tool in their hands. And when I speak of his board of strategy I do not include Mr. Drew.
I come to federal politics. As, five years ago, the present leader of the opposition spoke as the premier of his province, to-day he spoke in this house as the leader of a great dominion party-using "great" in a manner of speaking, but there are still great men in it. And if the Conservative party-call it "Progressive Conservative", "Tory", or what you will-is not stronger to-day in this country, it is because the hon. gentleman has listened to the voices of those who, though they cannot be elected by the people of Canada, continue to run the group. I regret that that is so, because they are bigoted and narrow-minded, while the hon. gentleman himself is broadminded and is not bigoted. Those men are responsible for the division which exists in this country. If the hon. gentleman spoke
The Budget-Mr. Pouliot

to them with the same aggressiveness and forcefulness as he spoke to-da}1, in this house I am sure there would be no more articles in the Ontario papers against the province of Quebec. It is pretty tough to listen to the predicants of national unity. National unity does not exist in this country. It is unfortunate; no one regrets it more deeply than I do. Unity will exist when the two old parties get rid of those who, as I have proved to the house, pull the strings for their own benefit. These men have not the confidence of the people, and how can the leader of the opposition expect to regain the confidence of the people by listening to the Jonahs who have been rejected by the whale, reflected; not only once, as was the Jonah of the old testament, but every time they faced the people? Even the big whale could not swallow them.
I heard the hon. gentleman speak of cooperatives. He has views on the subject, which no doubt I shall read about in the five o'clock papers. It was impossible to take a note of what he said. There may be some good suggestions in what he said on that subject, and if so they may be taken into account by the government. But with regard to the wheat pools he knows very well that the price which the grain growers get for their wheat now on the London market is $1.55.

speechtext: At Fort William.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: London is a different story.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, but there are subsidies. When I look over the border I find that the price of wheat is $2.15 or $2.18. The United States price is a little higher. That is because our trade channel is up a dead-end street, or a one-way street. I leave that for meditation by the hon. gentleman, who can draw his own conclusions and communicate them to his friends of the elevators of the west.
But how can the hon. gentleman complain about taxation and extravagance? Here are the first two points emphasized in his amendment by the financial critic for the opposition:
(1)	That the budget does not provide for tax reductions in the calendar year ,1946;
(2)	That the budget gives no indication of any serious attempt to eliminate extravagance or effect economies in the cost of government.
It was easy to practise economy, but once again the Conservative party has missed the boat. When the loan policy was brought to the house it was found that it was wrong. The Conservative party approved it. They approve anything that is going to be done for other countries. I am not so bigoted as to say that we should do nothing for others, but in one respect I agree with R. B. Bennett when 
be said "Canada first"; I believe that Canada should be served first and that others should be served by Canada only after Canada has been well served. So these gentlemen have not the right to complain about extravagance. I think of their own turpitude when they mention extravagance in their amendment. When I spoke of that in the house the newspapers had big headlines, "Quebec member opposed to British loan," thereby insinuating that the member for Temiscouata was antiBritish. I am not anti-British, but I am proCanadian. I see in all papers "Quebec" members have done this, "Quebec" members have done that. Always Quebec. Well, I decided to visit English-speaking Canadians outside of the house-in the Ottawa valley, in the St. Lawrence valley, and along the Atlantic coast, to the great city of Halifax. There I repeated exactly what I have said in this house

and what I say in my own county-because I have no different language for the one or the other. When I believe something I say it, whether I am wrong or right, and I admit I am wrong when I am proved to be wrong; but that has not occurred yet. I have the happiest recollection of a meeting which I had the honour to address when I told my audience that what was lacking in the House of Commons was the Canadian spirit, which should be the inspiration of our legislation. I did not say anything unpleasant about my colleagues. I said of them, sir-and I included yourself- that they were a fine bunch of fellows, which is true. It is unfortunate however that men of good will belonging to all parties in the house very seldom succeed in having their serious and most valuable suggestions adopted. In some mysterious way success comes to those on the outside. When a member of parliament makes an academic speech it does not go any farther than the house; but if an outsider, who has the halo of an expert, becomes an adviser to the government, at once his word is gospel and he must be listened to. This is very dangerous.
I said a moment ago that the Rowell-Sirois commission was a fiesta of the intelligentsia. All the people that could be got together from all around came to give, not evidence, but presentations, and they suggested all sorts of things. Most of the time it was not in the public interest, but in their own personal interest, to present a fine bill, to be well paid, and to see the little job or the fat job on the horizon coming to them just as quickly as possible. That was the purpose.
How can the hon. gentleman who leads the opposition, and his supporters, complain about bureaucracy? The Rowell-Sirois report is the magna charta of bureaucracy in Ottawa. That

The Budget-Mr. Low
is the trouble, and if we wish to redress wrongs of the past we must undo the workings of the Rowell-Sirois commission and we must return to what we were before the adoption of that report in an oblique way.
I am not going to speak much longer, although I have much more to say; but I mention again the Canadian spirit. The Canadian spirit should be our inspiration, and I say to some of my colleagues who were born outside, but who are Canadians at heart, as well as to all those who were born in this country: imperialism is the political religion of men without a country. Imperialism does not appeal to youth and at the present time there are two ways which are open to youth, one of which lies in the way of thinking that characterized our forefathers. It is the red-blooded Canadian way, the basis of which is patriotism rooted in the land of birth or adoption, above everything else. That is patriotism. But patriotism has long since been discarded, to be replaced by imperialism and then by internationalism; and internationalism is the synonym of communism. And, I say to my hon. friends, the other way that is open to youth is communism. I am in direct contact with the people and I know what our youth are thinking. I know what the returned boys are thinking. I know what the boys who stayed at home and were busy in essential occupations also know. Those boys are better Canadians than previous generations, and by that I mean that they think more of this country than is evident here in this house.
Take for instance the question of the flag. The public sentiment has not been understood by those who have designed a monstrosity which has no meaning, because the purpose of a flag is to be the sign-the "ensign", or the sign-of a country, and of one country in particular, without any subjection or suggestion of hegemony in relation to any other country. I say public sentiment was not understood. It was not understood so well in this house, under this roof, as it is understood by the youth of the country, and I hope that when the time comes to make a choice, that choice will not be made in camera but in the open, so that the sentiments that are necessarily in the hearts of men of good will will appear, and youth will choose a real Canadian flag instead of the red flag with hammer and sickle.
Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River): It is because the rules of the house forbid the Social Credit group moving an amendment that I wish to speak for a few minutes to-day in order to clarify our position both with respect to the motion and on the amendment moved by my hon. friends the Conservatives. I am
sure hon. members will not feel that I an holding up the business of the house undulj if I take a few minutes to clarify our position That would have been done had we been able to move a subamendment.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley), speaking in this debate a few days ago, expressed his desire to reach as soon as possible a position where he could bring in a balanced budget. That desire is quite understandable and from the personal point of view it would be for him something of an achievement. It certainly is a goal that has been sought by nearly every Minister of Finance. Moreover, by balancing the budget the minister would remove a great deal of the criticism that is usually levelled at him by the opposition in this house and throughout the country. Pressure toward a balanced budget has always been strong, and that is particularly so after a vast spending spree such as is exhibited during a destructive war.
I should like to point out that grave danger is involved in the determination to balance the federal budget. That does not hold so true with respect to provincial budgets, but it does with respect to a federal budget, especially because there is another way out. The minister should take warning that any undue pressure or haste on his part to balance his budget might result in a period of deflation. If such a trend is induced through the demands of unthinking opposition to the government, then I say it is inevitable that Canada's gross national production will be forced down to low levels, and that means only one thing, a low standard of living, depression, bread lines and human misery in a land of potential abundance. The federal government should resolve to do everything within its power to see that Canadian production of all kinds is kept at a high level. In my judgment, Sll billion a year is a reasonable minimum objective at the present time. The objectives should be revised from time to time as our productive capacity increases.
This government will come to realize sooner or later that balanced budgets will never meet the needs of a modern mass production economy so long as we continue under the system of financing which we now have. Balanced budgets in the federal field are bound to be restrictive in their effect, restrictive in every way. I refer to the traditional budget in which expenditures are brought within the revenues which the government expects.
I come now to the question of economy as it relates to the budget, and about which we have heard so much in the debate up to this day. Particularly I want to present it as if relates to a possible balancing of budgets.
The Budget-Mr. Low

The Social Credit group in this house has always advocated economy; but by "economy" we mean efficiency of expenditure and management within our country's ability to produce goods' and services. We do not mean undue pressure to cut down expenditures, to bring into balance those expenditures with anticipated tax revenues. The weakness of the Conservative position, as I understand it from their amendment, is that they press strongly for reduced government expenditures; but, as has already been pointed out, at the same time they advocate increased services to the people. The only possible result of such a position is a period of depression, a period of deflation. As the Conservatives learn more about the weaknesses of our money system they will come to understand that this is so.
The weakness of the C.C.P. position is just what the Minister of Finance pointed out last Thursday. They advocate huge government spending, but their only suggested alternative to high taxation is government ownership of the means of production from which they say there will accrue to the government profits with which services will be extended to the people without higher taxation.

speechtext: Plus greater production.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: An examination of the results of socialist rule in any country to this day will reveal the fact that while in many of these countries, notably New Zealand and Australia, increased social services have been extended to the people, they have been extended as a result of higher taxation. In no single country to this day can the C.C.F. demonstrate that the application of the socialist principle of government ownership 'has enabled the government there to extend social services without increased taxation. In her apology the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mrs. Strum)-and I took it as an apology on behalf of Australia and New Zealand- did enumerate the services that these countries are giving. I appreciate those services; I believe everyone appreciates to the full the increased services that those countries are giving. They have done very well in this respect, but it is only fair to point out that nowhere on the face of the earth are tax levels and per capita national debt so high as they are in those countries. What is more, even under socialist governments, economies have bogged down into periods of depression where great quantities of goods and services have wasted, while human beings have languished in want because they have not the means to buy.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Where has that happened?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In Australia and New Zealand. I say that the C.C.F. position is very weak indeed and is certainly no comfort to debt-burdened, tax-ridden and freedom-loving people.
As a contrast to the other two opposition parties, the social crediters have been consistent in showing the government where the money is to come from. Whenever we have advocated increased services to the people we have repeatedly urged the government to exercise the sacred responsibility which was placed upon them by the British North America Act to have a financial commission, or in the alternative, the Bank of Canada, issue for them debt free all the purchasing power required by all Canadians to do their business. The Minister of Finance, the governor of the Bank of Canada, and many other authorities admit that this can be done scientifically; that it is simply a matter of which way the people choose. History records that many times this method has been used in the past to the entire satisfaction of the people. Even the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Sinclair) who spoke just before one o'clock, can see how wrong it would be for people to go hungry when large quantities of foodstuffs are being utterly wasted in Canada simply because starving people have not the purchasing power with which to buy the goods. Even he could understand the action of his own government if they should create and issue to these people who are starving, who are in want, the amount of money which represents the value of these goods so that they could be consumed and the people kept from starving. I say, "even the hon. member for Ontario" in all friendliness.
The Social Credit party has been the realistic one, and it is now realistic. We know perfectly well that this time would be a poor one to create and issue additional new money. We have not advocated such a thing under present conditions of consumer goods shortage; we are not now advocating such a thing, but we have advocated more goods. Open wide the floodgates of production by removing every possible restriction to production so that goods and services can quickly come into balance with the money that is available to buy them. This is the only sensible way to meet the threat of inflation. It is the way we have consistently advocated. It is only when goods and services, not to come, but already in existence, cannot be bought by the people who need them, that we advocate issuing any new money, debt-free. But when we do suggest and advocate that it be issued we ask that it be issued in sufficient quanti-

The Budget-Mr. Low
ties to bring consumption and production into balance and keep them there. If that is done we will take the hills and hollows out of the economy over the years.
Social crediters have always declared that the bond-debt method of government financing is the most wasteful, inefficient and unfair method that can be adopted. To my knowledge-and I have searched earnestly for the information-its advocates have never yet been able to show that this system is anything but what I have already said: wasteful, inefficient and unfair.
I understand the objects of the bond-debt method of government financing; and I am speaking of it now entirely separate and apart from the taxation method. It has two objects. In the first place, its object is to encourage thrift, and with that I can quite agree. The second object is ostensibly to manage the money supply so that there will always be purchasing power in amounts to suit the needs of the people. The idea is that in good times, when things are going along swimmingly, the government will sell bonds, thereby withdrawing purchasing power and in some respects controlling the possibilities of inflation. In bad times the idea is to buy back the bonds and thereby put into circulation new money, thus increasing the purchasing power of the people generally.
A number of obvious weaknesses are apparent to anyone who will study this whole matter and its effects. When the government sells bonds, those securities will inevitably within a very short time find themselves in the hands of those who do not need the money to buy goods and services out of current production. I have already pointed out in this debate that if a mass production economy is to serve the people in this day, then mass production must be matched by mass consumption. I have also pointed out the poorly distributed purchasing power one -would find in Canada if a survey were carried out, as a survey was carried out in the United States. Another speaker in this debate has pointed out the poor distribution of pent-up war-time savings upon which business is depending so much for future orders. I say that mass consumption cannot be brought about if large groups of our population find themselves without adequate purchasing power to meet their needs. Under such circumstances goods will be wasted.
The second weakness of the bond-debt method of financing is that it diverts investment money from the development of resources in our country into the sure-thing investment field of government bonds. We often wonder why we are not getting the 63260-237
development of Canadian resources we ought to have. It is simply because we are opening the door wide to investment in government bonds by offering the people a sure thing at a good rate of interest. That becomes a drain away from investment in the resources of the country, to the extent that our resources cannot be developed as they ought to be under private enterprise. Of course private enterprise is blamed. To many people socialism seems to be inevitable because of our failure to recognize this weakness of the bond-debt financing system. Correct this weakness and socialism will cease to become a threat.
The third weakness is that the system actually accelerates and aids maldistribution among our citizens. Only a few people during their lifetime can afford to buy. government bonds or securities. The natural resultant of that is the fourth weakness. It creates a special social evil by making it possible for some men to live off the mortgaged toil of their fellow men. No man is entitled to that right.
The fifth weakness of the system is that it piles up burdens of unpayable debt, because of the high interest involved. I have already pointed out that, even in peace time, when one would expect we might be able to do something about the matter, this country did not even pay the interest on the debt we piled up. From 1919 to 1939, roughly the peace period between the two wars, this country increased its debt by almost the exact amount of the interest payable on the debt, which simply meant that we could not meet the interest, let alone whittle down the principal to anything like decent proportions.
The sixth weakness of the bond-debt method of financing is that it makes continued high taxation necessary. When the Canadian people face the future realizing that every year they will have to dig up through taxation $481,000,000 for interest on the debt, they can see little hope for anything like a period of freedom, a period of full enjoyment of the resources of our country. The only way we shall ever be able to deal adequately with a situation of that kind is to change our method, to get at the balancing of the purchasing power in the country with the production of the country in another way; and that way Social Credit has consistently and constantly advocated. If some hon. members, as they have said, have been sitting in this house for years without coming to understand Social Credit, that is because they have not applied their minds to it. People who have applied their minds have found that the solution is sound; and once they see, they become ardent advocates and devotees of the principles we advocate.

The Budget-Mr. Low

Bond-debt financing stands condemned as a means of managing the distribution of purchasing power within our country. The best evidence of its failure is the fact that over the years since it was first introduced the economies of all nations that have adopted it have been torn by periods of disastrous, recurring depressions, and by increasing loads of debt and taxation upon the people. Let me repeat that when social crediters advocate any additional government expenditures we shall always help the minister by showing him where he can get the money without resorting to additional taxation.
Now, Mr. Speaker, just one word about cooperatives before I conclude. The social crediters do not waste their time in trying to bring the tax burden of everyone, including the cooperatives, up to the same high level. What we should all be spending our time on is in finding a means of bringing the load of taxation on all individuals and businesses down to the level of the taxes paid by cooperatives. We should be doing something sensible if we did that. Social crediters will do everything within their power to protect the cooperatives from injury through taxation; and we shall have more to say on the specific resolutions when they come up, following the vote on the budget. With the reservations I have already mentioned, the Social Credit group propose to vote for the amendment because of what it says and not because of what some people might interpret the wording to mean.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget under discussion is perhaps the most unpopular budget ever brought down by a Canadian government. It is particularly unpopular with the average Canadian, who looked for a great deal but finds very little in the budget proposals to be happy about. While the minister refers to the severity of the attacks on the budget by members of this house, and perhaps feels that such attacks are unjustified, the lea4ers of the cooperative movement and cooperative associations across this country have used very strong language in their criticism of the budget proposals in regard to cooperatives. I have here, in the Manitoba Cooperative, an editorial entitled "Discrimination", which says:
The viciousness of the proposed legislation contained in the 1946 resolutions is aimed at the eventual destruction of the cooperative organizations.
Taking into consideration the number of letters and telegrams I have received, I am sure the leaders of cooperatives across the country are unanimous in their opposition to 
the budget proposals in this connection. I could continue quoting from various articles along the same line appearing in the press, but I shall deal with this phase of the budget later on in my remarks.
I should like to compliment the minister on the very hard work he put into the preparation of the budget. My honest conviction is that no one in Canada has given more of his time and effort in the service of Canada than has the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley). The most unfortunate thing is, however, that so much was expected of this budget and so little relief has come in the way of taxation or in the laying down of a real peacetime economy. It is like the old saying that "the mountain has laboured and brought forth a mouse".
At page 3589 of Hansard the minister says:
The C.C.F. opposition has shown no concern about our expenditures.
He continued by saying:
I enjoy listening to them; but they never come down to this: How would they finance? That is the question they never answer.
Hon. members have complimented the minister upon his capitalist budget. I agree that it is well-nigh impossible for any capitalist government to give anything little better than rationed poverty to the masses of the people, and still permit the legalized robbery of the farmers and workers of this country. A capitalist government is put into power primarily to protect capital, and so far in this country the voters have been successfully misled by people like Trestrail and have voted for capitalist governments. In Great Britain the people have decided, in the traditionally British and progressive way, to chart a new course. There they have voted in a government with an economic policy similar to that of the C.C.F. [DOT]

speechtext: Nothing like it at all.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I did not hear anyone advocating, and especially before the last election, that Canada should follow in the traditions of Great Britain. However, among other things I wish to cover two main points. First, I wish constructively to criticize the government for its failure in governmental policy, and in regard to the present budget, for its failure for laying a basis of a high and enduring standard of living for our people, and to show them what can be done under democratic socialism.
Second, I wish to deal with some of the specific resolutions in regard to the cooperatives. I see that the minister is not in his seat at the moment, but I believe, if he will forget

The Budget-Mr. McCullough
the capitalist viewpoint, that I can illustrate the democratic socialist way whereby a high standard of living can be achieved for all our people.
At the very beginning of the minister's speech the other day he said, as recorded at page 3589 of Hansard:
Most of the speeches have been directed to the urging of measures which would help here and there, but few of the speeches that have come from the opposition parties in this debate have taken into account the necessity of keeping within our means.
Again, to quote from his remarks at page 3596, he said:
We can go ahead and incur huge deficits, and do everything that everybody wants for a while if we can get people to lend us the money.
These two statements coming from the minister seem like an echo of the pre-war Liberal government policy:	Where is the money
coming from? Much praise has been taken by the government for their war effort, instead of attributing such success to the efforts of the people, which have been magnificent. However, the people of the country, after giving their services for the winning of the war, and producing the goods of war, now find that they have tied to their necks a millstone of a national debt of $16 billion, and an annual tribute of around $481 million to the capitalist class of this country. I think, if a true answer could be given as to who has won this war, it would not be the returned serviceman who to-day is looking for a home and finds he has to pay twice what it was worth before he finds one, or the worker who is trying to fight for a decent wage. It would be the privileged few who have had cost-plus contracts, and who now greedily demand the same privileges of profit.
I wish to hasten to say here that I do not believe that all capitalists are terrible ogres without soul or conscience. But to-day, as down through the centuries, we are fighting a class struggle. Some of us are on the side of the common people, while some are on the side of special privileges. Since we have said this has been the war of the common man, then to interpret that into real victory it would mean that so far as Canada was concerned there would need to be, considering that we had relatively full employment during the war, at least the creation of 600,000 new jobs for the
800,000	people in the armed services. This would allow 200,000 to be absorbed through marriage, in the permanent .army and in other ways. Then we could really say we had full employment.
These 600,000 new jobs would have to be in addition to jobs for those employed in war industry during the war, who would on recon-63260-237i
version have to have jobs. Nothing short of scientific planning can accomplish this, nothing short of the responsibility of the government realizing that everyone has a right to work, and accepting the principle that full employment means more jobs than applicants. This is not possible under capitalism. Capitalism can function only on a large float of unemployed.
I wish to bring two- examples before the house, one of which is taken from the Bankers' Magazine of London for August, 1943. It
states:
Workers of the future will require fears of unemployment and poverty to ensure the necessary drive in this world of internal and international competition.
Another quotation taken from the London Times of January 23, 1943, states:
Unemployment is not a mere accidental blemish in a private enterprise economy. On the contrary, it is part of the essential mechanism of the system, and has a definite function to fulfil.
The first function of unemployment (which has always existed in open or disguised forms) is that it maintains the authority of master over man.
Under the capitalist system the minister has only two main sources of revenue, those of taxation and borrowing. The average person is burdened with taxes for this and taxes for that until he cannot stand any further taxation. Big business and monopoly are still running this country. They will be taxed pretty well just as much as they choose and no more. So that the minister is in a quandary as how to give old age pensioners superannuation at sixty years of age, how to give free national health services and still keep taxes down on big business and allow them their profit.
I have regard for the minister in his plight, but I am far more concerned about the people, tens of thousands of them, and more joining the ranks every day, who realize that if everyone was allowed to work and that if wages and prices were fair, every Canadian would be assured of a decent standard of living, that we could have adequate old age pensions at sixty years and free health care for all our people.
Let us look back over history. I said earlier that we have had a class struggle down through the ages. May I say that for scores of centuries the world's wealth producers were mostly the property of an owning class- chattels, slaves. Some one wrote that "next to the preservation of life itself, the craving for freedom is the dominating objective of all conscious life." Slaves wanted freedom and frequently rebelled. One such rebellion led to Sparticus, a slave gladiator, who defied
The Budget-Mr. McCullough

the power of Rome for about three years. When this rebellion was quelled, the fear-maddened owners used frantic cruelty. Along the Appian way, six thousand crosses were planted and six thousand slaves were nailed to them.
Changing methods of production and fear of rebellions gradually brought owning classes to adopt changes, first to serfdom, and then to the free wage serf. They reasoned something like this. Slaves and serfs must have enough of their own products to keep them in fit condition to work and they must also raise children to keep up the supply of workers. Why not give them full freedom and hire them for a wage that will allow them to buy their own living? We will give them the form of freedom. As long as we own the means of life, namely the natural resources and the machinery of production, transportation and distribution for the primary producer, we will hold ownership of the markets where they must buy and sell. By owning these, we can keep for our own use all they produce above what it costs them to live. We will let them imagine that they are free and we need no longer fear heavy rebellions. There you have the greatest hoax in all history. George Bernard Shaw, with his usual caustic wit, called this hoax "giving the workers the key to the street."
We have the form of freedom, but economically we are the slaves who produce our own living and also the luxury living of the owning class. In addition, we have built up, with the labour of our hands and brains, the great industrial, transportation and distribution systems that exist in the world today. We have done all this for slaves' pay and a wage for our labour and a price for our product that would on the average buy us a living.
The present great wealth producing systems are, legally-because the owning class have always been able to make the laws-the property of a small owning class. About all we own is the right to produce wealth when the owning class can use our labour or buy our products at a profit. If anyone should question this I would refer him to the labour disputes that we read about in the newspapers, where wage increases are demanded by workers and only conceded by employers when it can be proven that the cost of living has gone up. The fact that the workers are producing a large surplus above their cost of living wage does not seem to be considered much by either side.
I would remind hon. members that in Canada, of which we are all so proud, we have achieved in the past year our greatest national

production of $11 billion. In the light of that, the standard of living in this country is disturbing. I have here the Labour Force Bulletin, put out by the Department of Labour, which shows that in 1945, excluding those in the armed forces, we had 4,256,000 people gainfully employed in Canada. In the Canadian Unionist of May, I find another table. By doing a little bit of arithmetic I find that of the 4,256,000 who were gainfully employed in 1945, those earning over $2,000 numbered 687,700, and the number earning $2,000 or less who were gainfully employed was 3,568,300. Subtracting those earning less than $2,000 but paying income tax from the total labour force, exclusive of the armed services, gives us 1,891,000 people or approximately forty-four per cent of the total population gainfully employed who do not qualify to pay income tax under the exemptions of $660 or $1,000 for single and married men respectively, and eighty-four per cent earn under $2,000. This confirms that even in this country we have not the freedom we should have when we are capable of producing a gross national income of $11 billion.
I have contended that a capitalistic government gets the money for social services and government expenditure mainly from two sources, by borrowing and taxation. I wish to illustrate how a democratic socialist government, such as the C.C.F. advocate, would get the money and how the standard of living of our people would be governed only by the availability of labour applied to our resources. In other words, what is physically possible would be made financially possible. The minister has challenged us on that. Let me illustrate by taking first the capitalist set-up and then what could be done under the democratic socialist set-up.
Let us take as an example, a large factory in a capitalist set-up. Here the owner pays the wages and other overhead in the cost of producing the goods. As an example, in a shoe factory the wages are paid, and taxes and overhead are all the responsibility the factory owner has. Then the owner has the legal right to all the shoes produced, less his costs. Under modern technology this means he accumulates wealth when he sells the surplus shoes, wealth which, unless reinvested, remains out of circulation. The owner can wear only one suit of clothes and one pair of shoes at a time, and even if he lives in the most riotous luxury he can spend only a small portion of his profit. Consequently huge accumulations of wealth become built up, which ordinarily are not reinvested and do not come into circulation. This means that under private monopoly huge accumulations of

The Budget-Mr. McCullough
wealth become centralized. The same is true of our large financial institutions where, through usury, money is accumulated and concentrated.
In this example of the shoe factory, which is typical of all modern factories, we have the workers receiving only a small portion of the total wealth produced. It is clear to see that, if we use this reasoning for all industry, huge surpluses of goods of various kinds are produced without aggregate wages paid to buy back what is produced. This in the past has been the chief reason for exporting. Countries have had to fight for world markets, sometimes going to extremes in the struggle for markets, even to the extreme, one might say, of attempting to sell woollen underwear to the Africans or longer shirt-tails to the Chinese. Eventually capitalism breaks down, and it is true that the last two great wars were fundamentally fought for markets. This sort of process under capitalism forces periods of economic stagnation and collapse, periods which are coming closer and closer together. Here, too, is the reason for unemployment and the failure of capitalist governments to give the opportunity of full employment.
Let me illustrate by another example. In the A. O. Smith body plant at Milwaukee, Wisconsin, 20,000 employees originally employed produced a unit of 10,000 car frames a day. Then, around 1930 they built a semiautomatic plant which required only 2,000 men to produce the same unit of 10,000 car frames daily. A few years later, a fully automatic plant was built requiring only 200 men, or a displacement, in the production of this daily unit of 10,000 car frames, of 19,800 men. This has taken place over some thirty years of industrial and technological development. Under the capitalist system the owner has no responsibility for those 19,800 unemployed men. They are thrown into the lap of the government and become its responsibility. So that to-day, even though it be argued that plant working conditions are the very best, where there is air conditioning, good hours of work and good pay, it is still essential to socialize such industries, because private ownership of these factories gives too much financial and economic control over the lives of our people.
The minister has said that no one has told him where the money is to come from. I think I can tell him where it would come from if the people owned these factories. The wealth, instead of belonging to a legally privileged class, would belong to the people.

speechtext: Would the hon. member suggest that, if the country were under socialism, plants should not be modernized and equipped with the very best and most up-to-date machinery that could be got to cut down the cost of production?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I absolutely agree that that should be done.

speechtext: Well then, what you have said just now does not bear out at all the answer you gave me.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, it does. What we would use would be all the technological and scientific knowledge we have. We would be able to use these factories and these technological advances and improvements to have mass production, pay good wages in these factories, and have fair hours of work too. As I pointed out in giving this example of a shoe factory, when we had paid good wages to these people and sold enough shoes for that purpose, the shoes which remained would belong to the people, and, when they are sold, the money would go into the consolidated revenue of the country, and we would be able to provide social services, old age pensions and other things. There would be opportunities, for everyone willing to work at real jobs with decent wages. All would have a real incentive to work, and our national production would be governed only by the will to work. I do not think the minister can properly criticize this proposition of publicly owned enterprises or contend that they are less efficient than those privately owned, for I believe the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) has said that government-owned plants operated more efficiently than private companies during the war.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He never said any such thing.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In closing this part of my argument, let me say to the minister and to the government there has, in my opinion, never been a greater betrayal of the people than that of using the taxpayers' money in building up billions of dollars' worth of plant and equipment for war and then to scrap or sell them at fire-sale prices when these could have been converted to peace-time use and met the crisis of peace production as they met the crisis of war.
Instead of that, what have we to-day? Rather than enabling the small wage-earner to be * free from income tax, so that at least we could have income exemption of $1,000 for a single person and $2,000 for a married couple, $50 a month for men over sixty years of age
The Budget-Mr. McCullough

and women over fifty and free health services for all our people, we now find the minister and his government trying unsuccessfully to balance the budget. As I said before, the interest alone on our national debt is approximately the total pre-war government expenditure. The present financial policy is ridiculous and stupid.
To-day there is nothing but unrest, nothing but fear of the future. The question arises, what could and should be done to prevent this?
First, the government should have set up a federal planning board representative of organized labour and farmers, industry and government, Scientific surveys should have been made to find out the productive need1 of the country ; the potential productive capacity; possible employment in each field; proper basis of producer prices and wage levels, arrived at by negotiation. But what has the government done in this respect? It would seem that the only authority for planning is the wartime prices and trade board, carried over from the war. I have no quarrel with the personnel of this board, except to say this. I'f this board is to have power deliberately to raise farm costs and living costs without responsibility to parliament, I protest most strongly. We should have a national planning board with representation of organized agriculture and labour and industry and government, and this board should be responsible to parliament. Such a board, working in conjunction with the Minister of Finance, would be able to dispel the growing fears of our people and it would carry democracy into our national planning as never before.
As I have already said, the increase in exemptions allowed the people in the low-income brackets leaves the people no better off than they were a few years ago because everything has gone up to such an extent.
I cannot join in the optimism of the minister over his budget, I consider that such a budget will eventually lead to the government finding it necessary to protect big business by the government's emergency powers; it will find increasing unemployment, and unrest will force the government to use strong-arm methods to keep so-called law and order. To speak quite candidly, it will force the government to use measures of fascist tendencies; for fascism is only ultra-capitalism, capitalism in its last stages when capitalist forms of government are protected at any cost, where religious hatred or race baiting is thrown in to confuse the issue, but where, as I say, preservation of specilal privilege is the supreme purpose.

I wish now to deal with cooperatives. I want to add my voice to the strenuous objections taken by the leaders of the cooperatives across Canada in their criticism of the budget proposals in regard to cooperatives. Unless we can persuade the government to change, certain of these proposals, it portends sinister things to come. Because of certain proposals, I feel, that the budget strikes at the very basis of cooperation and would cripple the cooperative movement across this country.
Some cooperatives have vigorously objected, and I am in agreement with them on the following five points:
First, the objection taken that the proposals ignore the basic difference between cooperatives and private business. The cooperative organizations stem out of the need of the people who have cooperated to give themselves, through cooperation, services of various kinds at cost which they could not have got in any other way. The great wheat pools have grown up because farmers found that only by handling their wheat could they get a fair share of the products of their labour. The pools were organized, and the farmers through the pool elevators gave competition to the private elevators. There were spreads of ten and twelve cents between street and track prices; and handling charges were excessive. Through their pool organizations the farmers have been able to reduce the spread between street and track wheat to about two cents, and to reduce their handling charges materially. We farmers who are members of the pool consider the marketing of our wheat part of our farming operations. We have production costs of summer-fallowing, sowing, threshing and handling. We consider the marketing of our grain part of our business. We feel that the net price received by us should be the only money taxable, that it should be computed as part of farm income and that there should be no duplication of taxation. I maintain that in a bona fide cooperative there is no such thing as profit. The budget proposals fail to ensure that such organizations are tax exempt and leave cooperatives in doubt as to where they stand.
I could mention the Saskatchewan oil cooperative. Here again the farmers and cooperators joined together to cut down the cost of oil to themselves by setting up a cracking plant, and refining and distributing oil to themselves, thus making savings.
Resolution No. 12 would repeal section 4 (p) which recognized the differences between cooperatives and non-cooperatives. It would

The Budget-Mr. McCullough
be serious if the government failed to define this difference. I criticize the government for not having introduced a national cooperative act long ago. Then there would be no doubt as to what constituted a bona fide cooperative.
My second criticism is the objection that the proposals force cooperatives to treat members and non-members alike. This strikes at the very heart of the cooperative movement. What justification can there be to force a cooperative to treat non-members who have not any financial or other responsibility for such a cooperative on the same basis as members?
I take strong objection to this, and the very least the government should do is to allow a cooperative the choice of treating members and non-members alike, or, as an alternative, withholding dividends from nonmembers and paying a tax on the amounts so withheld. If non-members received the same treatment, since there would be no incentive to join and old members would die off, it would not be long before a cooperative would completely disintegrate. This is a vicious proposal.
The third objection is this, that the proposals would prevent cooperatives from providing service at cost by forcing them to pay tax on not less than three per cent of the employed capital. This prevents members from putting their money without interest into cooperative enterprise. This, too, is a discriminatory measure. As an example, take the position of a farmer who wishes with his neighbours to start a cooperative oil business. These farmers have already paid income tax on such money and, unless private business is taxed on the same basis, this tax is certainly unfair and discriminatory.
My fourth objection is that such proposals would interfere with the right of the individual member to leave his savings with his cooperative, for provision of further service, by forcing payment in cash within six months. By this being done, according to my information there is not enough time allowed to provide a safeguard so that cooperatives could limit or conduct their business in case of emergency, or depression, or other hazards. We shall suggest changes in committee. However, I think most cooperatives would be satisfied if the royal commission report on this matter were effected, whereby directors would have the power in any one year to limit the amount paid to ten per cent of the total and, temporarily, to suspend payments of patronage dividends in periods of crisis.
My fifth objection is this: They propose that the minister may, in his discretion, discriminate as between cooperatives in the matter of retroactive taxation. In listening
to the minister's speech and in reading it over, I am still at a loss, as I believe the minister and all members of this house are, to know what a bona fide cooperative is, and what cooperatives would be subject to retroactive taxation. Certainly no minister should have the right to decide mandatorily what is or is not a cooperative. The government has done a very great injustice in bringing in such proposals, which strike at the very basis of cooperation. It has failed to bring in a national cooperative act, defining a cooperative. Its failure to do this is as great as its failure to bring in a comprehensive national labour code. The people will not forget, unless the government repents and changes these proposals.
