speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Mr. L. PHILIPPE PICARD (Bellechasse) moved the second reading of bill No. 56, to amend certain acts in respect to the labelling and marking of foods and drugs.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LABELLING IN FRENCH AS WELL AS IN ENGLISH
speechtext: I should not like to deprive the hon. member of making a full explanation on the bill, and I am quite sure that he is prepared to do so.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LABELLING IN FRENCH AS WELL AS IN ENGLISH
speechtext:
I must really thank my hon. friend for his kind attention to me. This bill has been standing in my name since the 16th of April and we have had a long time to consider it. Since that time I have received comments for and against the bill and have discovered there was a strong feeling in favor of it. With the permission of the house I will give an idea of the motives behind the bill and state its intention and purpose.
At the moment the public throughout Canada is protected against fraud, misrepresentation and so on, under the Food and Drugs Act and it is protected against injury to health under the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act. The

Food and Drugs Act
object of the present bill is to provide for those who do not understand the English language the same protection as is provided under these two acts for those who speak English. It might be said by some that the labelling prescribed under the act is not for the purpose of warning the public as to the danger of the drugs so labelled; but if we look at section 3, paragraph (b), of the Food and Drugs Act it will be seen that it gives the governor in council power to enact legislation concerning different matters having to do with drugs and food. Paragraph (b) says that the governor in council has power to make regulations:
respecting the packaging and labelling of any article or food or drug and the design of any such package or label with a view to preventing the public or the purchaser-
I draw particular attention to these words:
-being deceived or misled as to the character, strength, quality or quantity of the article.
And so on. What I intend by this bill is to make sure that the probably 2,000,000 people in Canada who are not conversant with English and who therefore are not protected, as is the intention of the law be protected by including after "labelling" the words "in English and in French." I do not think the wording of the clause is correct and, if ever my bill reaches the committee stage, I would ask a colleague to move a motion to change the wording to make it more effective. I would ask to have moved at the end of paragraph (b) the following proviso:
Provided that if the governor in council makes any regulation respecting the labelling of any article of food or drug as above-mentioned said regulation shall provide for the labelling in the French as well as in the English language.
I would then have him move to strike from my bill the words "in English and in French" in the tenth and eleventh lines. That would make it clearer and more definite in its prospective application.
The next section of my bill, section 3 concerns the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act. Had I not been remiss in my duty I would have been here on Monday, May 20. It is often said that many members are away on Monday and Friday. Many will not admit it, but unfortunately I am forced to do so in the present case. I could then have proposed an amendment to the legislation that was passed by this house on that day to the same effect as I urge to-night, by moving to amend section 4 of bill No. 29, which now reads as follows:
(b) no retail druggist shall sell, or offer for sale except pursuant to direction of a physician, any- preparation referred to in paragraph (a) of this subsection unless there is printed in a conspicuous place on ah inseparable part of the
main panel of the label and wrapper of the bottle, box, or other container, and in letters of the same size and visibility as the directions for the use of the preparation, the full formula or true list of medicinal ingredients, and the following words: "It is unlawful to administer this preparation to a child under two years of age as it contains codeine and is dangerous to its life."
I should have moved that after the words "unless there is printed" there be added "in English and in French". However, on May 20 I was in my constituency and not in the house, and I have only myself to blame if I did not move my amendment then.
If it is judged by this house that it is wise to pass a law which forces manufacturers of drugs to warn the public that the preparation should not be administered to a child under two years of age, are we not just carrying on a humanitarian gesture by adding this same proviso, printed in the language of a large part of the population of Canada, a proportion of whom do not know the English language? I will not to-night enter into a long discussion about the rights and merits of the French against the English, or the inalienable rights of this or that section; no, it will not be such a speech; I am only asking that protection be given to those who, according to the laws of this country, are entitled to speak their language, that in respect of the warnings given under the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act and the safeguards provided by the Food and Drugs Act, they receive the same protection as is given those who know English.
I shall not enter into a long discussion of that matter. The point is just this, shall we or shall we not recognize that, in accordance with their undoubted rights, some people in this country are not bilingual? There are some who are not bilingual because they know only English; there are other who are not bilingual because they know only French. If those who know only English are protected under the law, why should not those who know only French be protected? I do not think anybody would suffer if such protection were accorded, and it would be in the interests of the health of a large number of people in this country.
Hon. members may wonder Why I, who am not a physician, would worry about this; that I, who never attempted to ring the bell of nationalism or to build my following on arguing the rights of this or that minority- though I have done my best to defend and uphold them-should come forward to-night with such a bill? Well, it may be a long story but it is a childhood story. My father was a country doctor; or I should not say* a "country" doctor because he was a physician
Food and Drugs Act

at Riviere-du-Loup, the nicest little city in the world, so well represented by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot). My father practised there for twenty-five, years. At one time a client came to his office with his daughter, who was sick. My father prescribed a certain medicament; he had it in his own office; and at the time he was about to hand it to the patient's father he was called away to another patient and had to leave his home, so he said to this man, "You can read English. I give you the bottle, on which the dose is plainly and clearly written. Give it to the child according to those directions". He explained it to him in French, and the man, who could read English, went away. The health of the daughter improved; at least I suppose so, because my father was a good doctor. But some time later in the same home a young child got sick, and the girl's mother, the wife of the man who had received the bottle, did not read English, so she said, "If it was good for my other daughter, this seems to be the same ailment and I will give it to the child." But the medicine contained codeine or some such drug; the child got worse and my father was called in. When he came home my father, who was not one of these rabid nationalists, who was bilingual and had studied in England and in France, said, "Will the day ever come when both our people will have the same chance assured to them by law? Shall we ever have a law that will require the formulas on our medicaments to be printed in both languages?"
Later on, I happened to travel a bit, and went to Mexico, where, if I remember well, Your Honour was years ago. Travelling in that country and in Cuba, I saw that all the drugs imported to Cuba and Mexico, even those labelled on one side in English, had on the other side a label in Spanish containing a perfect translation, for which there was room enough on the bottles. That story of my childhood came (back to my mindi, and I investigated the field of medical preparations. I have discovered that, throughout the whole of Canada, probably thirty per cent of the drugs sold are labelled in both languages. This is due to the trade ability or good will of the manufacturers. It has taken time to reach that. I remember my father writing for this purpose to some of these firms, and now things have reached the point where I am assured by doctors that this practice is growing. An hon. member who is a physician and an English-speaking Canadian told me of seeing in Winnipeg a well-known drug the label of which, and not only the outside container, was printed in both languages.

As the matter stands at the moment, there being no law requiring protection for those who speak only French, we have chaos in the drug business. As I have said, in the whole of Canada only about thirty per cent of the drugs have directions printed in both languages. In Quebec, I would say the proportion is probably fifty per cent, and another fifteen per cent have outside labels in both languages, while the bottle is labelled only in English. So that you have four if not five ways in which these medicaments are labelled. Some issued by firms in the last five years are fully bilingual, which shows that it can be done without cost or trouble, besides being just and equitable to those who speak only French.
I have here an article from a certain firm. I am not advertising it; I am not selling its products; I do not know the proprietors; they are all nice people, but I do not care about any of them except, of course, when I need their products. One from Charles E. Frosst is called ostrogen. What it does I do not know, but anyway it is perfectly printed. The bottle is small; yet space has been found to put on it the formula in both English and French, and the warning as to how it should and how it should not be taken. These instructions are found not only on the wrapper but on a tiny bottle like the one I have in my hand, which shows that, with good will, there is no reason why any receptacle, however small, could not have the particulars printed in both languages.
Here is another bottle, even smaller, from Montreal, "Poulenc", a French firm which has opened branches in the United States and Canada.
Here we have a smaller container of "Gardenal", which I remember was mentioned in one of the answers given by the then minister when the Food and Drugs Act was proposed in 1920. It was stated that it was a narcotic and that the formula should be well printed or fully described. Anyway, on the package, small as it is, space has been found to put it in French and English, with the warning that it was a narcotic and should not be given without a doctor's prescription.
Here is one by a company operating in Switzerland, in Canada and in the United States, the CIBA company. This medicine I have here contains fully bilingual directions on the bottles, although they are very small. I chose the smallest bottles I could find to indicate that my proposal is a perfectly feasible one.
Here is another one, "Vick's" inhaler, made in the good city of Windsor, represented by my hon. friend the Secretary of State (Mr. JULY 23, 1946
Food and Drugs Act
Martin), who is three-fourths French, while I am seven-eighths French. There is just a matter of one-eighth between us, because I had a grandmother who was half English, which makes me one-eighth English, while he had an Irish grandmother. This drug made in Windsor is fully described both in English and French, and as will be seen, the package 'is very small.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LABELLING IN FRENCH AS WELL AS IN ENGLISH
speechtext: I am sure the hon. gentleman will permit me the observation that there is no doubt about the very high quality of that particular product.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LABELLING IN FRENCH AS WELL AS IN ENGLISH
speechtext:
I am sure of that; it comes from the home of my hon. friend. I know he was interested in drugs years ago, because I found his name in a debate on the question in 1936 or 1938. So that I am sure he will approve of me to-night.
I have another preparation here, or rather only the box. The bottle was big and I feared to drop it. This one is known as Collyrium and has a bilingual container outside. Although the bottle itself is big, apparently they could find space only for English. It is written in French and English on the outside box, but on the bottle you find only English. That is what is called a concession to Quebec, to please the Quebec trade. There is a second wrapper which is intended specially for the purchaser in Quebec. Presumably, when he is ou-tside Quebec he is supposed not to get sick. He does not even have to take aspirin tablets, because the makers of aspirin have not seen fit to have directions printed bilingually on the box or on the container but only on the Quebec cardboard.
Another preparation I have here is Alophen, which is put up by Parke, Davis.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LABELLING IN FRENCH AS WELL AS IN ENGLISH
speechtext: Is that Toronto?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LABELLING IN FRENCH AS WELL AS IN ENGLISH
speechtext: Walkerville.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LABELLING IN FRENCH AS WELL AS IN ENGLISH
speechtext: And also Windsor.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LABELLING IN FRENCH AS WELL AS IN ENGLISH
speechtext:
This also has an outside carton which is bilingual, and on the inside there appears this: "To comply with certain pharmacy acts, this bottle is labelled poison." There is a space which is left blank; evidently they were not prepared to print anything in French on it. On the bilingual outside container they forgot to put what they stated on the inside about poison.
Here is another one, to show the house the chaos we are in. I am referring to Phillip's milk of magnesia in tablets. Let me assure the house that I am not advertising anything; I am a lawyer, and although I may not be prosperous in the legal profession, I have no intention of going into the advertising business. However, here you find everything in English except the dose. They have printed the directions jor use in five lines of French, and that is something anyway, even if you dc not know what the preparation is taken for. You may not know what it is intended for, but you know how much you should take.
Here is another one: Grove's cold tablets. The same thing applies here. There are directions for use. They do not tell you what it is for, and no doubt you buy it for the sake of obtaining the nice white cardboard box. You know how many you should take, but not what they are for.
I have here other samples, the great majority of which are labelled only in English. That is the admitted general practice.
Here is something else that might be a menace to health, which is put up in the United States by that other company which I praised a moment ago for being bilingual in respect of what they sell in Canada, CIBA. So far as the American end of this company is concerned, it is established at Summit, New Jersey. Of course there is no question of speaking French either in their house of representatives or in their state legislature. If French is used in that country it is used as a mark of culture by certain classes, as it is in most countries of the world. This preparation is printed in English, and of course there is no question of imposing French upon the Americans in their country.
However, this product is imported into Canada, it is supposed to be for adults only, and the caution is given that it should not be used by individuals suffering from heart disease or thyroid disturbance except on the advice of a physician. This comes into Canada and no one is protected who does not speak English. Let us note that if there are two million people in this country who do not speak English, there are many more millions who do not speak French. Nevertheless, those who do not speak English have no protection so far as this preparation is concerned, while their English-Canadian compatriots are protected.
I suggest that if it is our desire to carry out the intent of the law it would be well for us to see what was stated in 1939 when the law was modified. At that time the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) was Minister of Pensions and National Health, and as reported at page 331 of Hansard of 1939, he made this statement:
Means are being sought-
That is, in the amendments which he was proposing at that time.
-to make more effective the restraints upon misrepresentation in the marketing of foods and drags.
Food and Drugs Act

But how can there be misrepresentation if you do not represent anything? If the cover of a container is blank to the one who reads it, no matter how cultured he may be in some other language, obviously he does not know what is represented in those printed words. The printed matter should appear in such a form that he can read it. Again, at page 822 of the same volume of Hansard, the minister said that the object of the amendments was:
To improve the statutory means for protecting the purchasing consumer against injury to health-
That would apply to the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act, which does not make it compulsory to state explicitly that the drug is not safe for any child.
-and against deception in food and drug products.
The aim of the act, according to the minister at that time, was to protect the consumer against injury to health. Injury would result if a young boy, whose parents did not read English, administered a drug to him in the absence of any caution printed in both languages. To attain the objects which the minister stated, authority was then sought: to deal in greater detail with matters such as packaging and labelling, advertising, adulteration and the use of dangerous materials.
I remember that in 1939 the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) told the minister about someone who had bought rat poison which somebody had eaten because there was no proper label on the container, and the minister assured him that under the act as it was then being amended labels would be printed in such a way that no one could possibly mistake rat poison for food. The hon. gentleman who told about the incident was apparently satisfied because his objection was limited to pointing out that particular case. But if it is considered necessary that a label should be printed in such a way as to ensure the protection of people who read the caution in English, why should not the same safeguard be afforded the two million people who do not speak English and who have the same rights under the law?
I am not going to take up any more of the time of the house, but I would appeal to the good will of all hon. members in this matter. Should, by chance, this bill go to a committee, I will bring in amendments to improve the law so as to provide for bilingual labelling so far as drugs only are concerned. Through inadvertence. I worded my bill in such a way that it would apply to foodstuffs as well. I do not wish to go that far, for the moment at any rate, because it might force some small British Columbia salmon packers

who market their product on the west coast of the United States and Canada to have their labels printed in French as well as English, and I do not suggest that that should be done, any more than I should like to have the people in my province who are packing small fruits for sale in neighbouring villages compelled to print their labels in both languages. My suggestion is that it should apply only to drugs. I assure the house that my intention is neither narrow nor nationalistic, but it is just for protecting our people that I wish to see these labels printed in French as well as in English. My object is to ensure the protection of those who speak only French, just as those who speak English are protected. I appeal to the minister and to the house to approve the principle involved, and if we get in committee I will propose the amendments necessary to bring the bill more in line with its aim.

speakeroldname: Hon. BROOKE CLAXTON (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LABELLING IN FRENCH AS WELL AS IN ENGLISH
speechtext:
The hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Picard) has given us a delightful speech in favour of this bill, subject to such further amendment as he may be prepared to make if the bill reaches the committee. In his speech he made a number of points which were of considerable interest to hon. members. He produced a substantial array of exhibits. Last year we had hon. members producing fruit of various kinds and we were told this was not a fruit store. In another legislative [DOT] place I remember seeing hon. members competing on the relative values of different types of club sandwiches, and since all the club sandwiches were juicy it created quite a scene.
The bill put forward by the hon. member must be considered on the text which is before us. Section 2 proposes an amendment which would enable the governor in council to make regulations respecting the packaging and labelling in English and in French of any article of food or drug. The existing regulations in force read in division 1, section 1, part A (1) as follows:
Every article of food or drug in packaged form sold or put up by the manufacturer or producer thereof shall be labelled.
That has been part of the law of Canada for a long time. It has been generally enforced to the satisfaction of the Canadian people. It is arguable that if the amendment means anything it means that, whenever any requirement is made regarding the labelling of any food or drug in Canada, the labelling should be in English and in French. It is also arguable that it may mean something else, but from what the hon. member said I would gather that it was his intention that

Food and Drugs Act
all labelling be in French and English. The hon. member has been good enough to say that that is not his intention so far as food is concerned. I think it would meet with
the wishes of the members of the house and of the buying public in Canada generally that it should not be necessary to label all articles of food in French and in English. To do so would lead greatly to the inconvenience of everyone and to the cost of doing business. Therefore, if we restrict the provisions of the bill as the hon. member suggests that he would have restricted it had it been drawn so as to give effect to his intention, then it should be restricted to require the labelling of drugs. I gather from what he says that he would propose that labelling of drugs should be carried out in French and in English.
We now come to the question of different classes of drugs. First, we have narcotics, which are dealt with under the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act. This was amended at this session of parliament to make the sale of all narcotic drugs possible only under prescription. Therefore a very large class of cases which the hon. member has in mind is covered by the existing legislation. In fact the case which he mentioned where his father gave a drug to somebody which was not properly used was, I understand, a case where codeine was the drug. Under the existing law that could only be done on the prescription of a doctor. If a doctor prescribes a drug there is no requirement in any law that his prescription should be in French and English. The prescription is aimed at the person who asks for it, and if a person speaks French the doctor makes the label on the bottle or the druggist makes the label on the bottle in French, or if the patient speaks English, then it is put on the bottle in English, or the physician and druggist are not likely to continue to enjoy the custom of that particular patient.
This year we brought into effect a law under which all narcotics of every type can be sold only on prescription, except very small doses of codeine which must be mixed with other drugs and which would be very unlikely to do any harm to anyone. These very small quantities of codeine can be sold without a doctor's prescription, but they must have a warning label in one language or the other. I would suggest that the only possible application of the hon. member's suggestion to narcotics would be to that small class of cases in which it is at least arguable that unless considerable quantities of the medicine are taken there would be little harm, even to a small child.
Then there are drugs other than narcotics in respect of which there are labelling provisions of the act and of the regulations. These labelling provisions are designed to give any purchaser an accurate description of the contents of the bottle or box which he is buying. It is submitted in that respect we can leave the choice of language very largely to the good sense of the customer and of the manufacturing chemist or other person producing that particular medicine for sale. If he wants to make a sale of the medicine to persons who speak the French language, then he has to put his label in French or he will not be so likely to make the sale. If he wants to make it to English-speaking people, then he should put it in English or he will not be so likely to make the sale. In that respect it is very much the same as in the Case of food. It is a matter where we can let the ordinary rules of customer-vendor relationship take effect so as to see that the person gets what he wants.
With regard to another class of drugs or medicines, namely poisons, the hon. member here is dealing with a matter which has been dealt with by the provinces. Every province has a pharmacy act. In Quebec the pharmacy act is chapter 267 of the revised statutes of 1935, and section 20 reads:
It shall be unlawful to keep or sell any of the poisons named in the said schedule, unless the box, bottle, vessel, wrapper or cover, in which such poison is contained, be distinctly labelled with the name of the article and the word "poison" and with the name and address of the seller of the poison.
The schedule to the act has a number of medicines listed many of which would not ordinarily be regarded as poisons, but which undoubtedly, if taken in sufficient quantity, would poison anyone. That is the requirement of the Quebec law; and. I believe that there is a corresponding requirement in the law of every province. In no province is there a requirement that this important warning be put in both languages.
I would suggest to the hon. member that a large part of his case has been met by the amendment proposed this year to the Narcotic Drug Act which has been enacted, and that such part of it as is left should properly be directed at the provinces which, under these pharmacy acts, make certain requirements with regard to medicines which may act as poisons. So I would respectfully submit to the hon. member that in view of the amendment made this year and in view of the situation in the provinces, where they have laws in force, the matter should be reconsidered, to see if there is any case which should be covered by legislation and which is not now covered.
Food and Drugs Act

.Just one word in conclusion, and it is this. I think it can be said that in the cases which have been drawn to the attention of our department where someone has been done an injury through taking some drug or medicine improperly or in excess, it is difficult to say that this has been due to any failure to read the label properly because it was not printed in both languages. In the majority of such cases the person taking the medicine could not read in any language because he or she was too young to read. I would submit that for every case where some injury has been done due to any failure to print the label in both languages, there are many cases due to the inability of the person to read in any language or to know what he is doing because of the age of that person; and there is no way in which laws can be drawn to safeguard infants of tender years against injuries done through negligence on the part of parents or doctors or druggists or others concerned with the handling of medicines and drugs. For our ultimate protection in regard to these matters we must look first, as we do, to the provincial laws regarding poisons, which I think are well drafted and adequately enforced and carried out; second, to the federal law regarding narcotics, which has been extended in consequence of legislation passed this year and is now, I think, effectively enforced; third, to the provisions regarding labelling, which I think to a greater degree in Canada than elsewhere are fairly enforced, to ensure that as far as possible a person buying a medicine knows what he is buying; buit ultimately we must look to the care of all the people who have to handle these things, and for that care no legislation can enforce or replace that care entirely.
So, Mr. Speaker, in the light of the changes brought about in the situation this year since the hon. member introduced his bill, and in the light of the representations I have made that this is so largely a matter falling within the jurisdiction of the provinces, I would ask the hon. member if he would withdraw his bill and consider if there still remains some field which could be adequately covered by legislation of this house.

speechtext: Did I understand the minister to state it was left to the province to decide whether articles of food as well as drugs should be labelled? I thought there was some misunderstanding, because any product of our province of British Columbia by its very pack is shown to be pure.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LABELLING IN FRENCH AS WELL AS IN ENGLISH
speechtext:
I have noted the expression of views by the minister. I do not know that I could entirely agree with him when he says the existing laws have been applied to the satisfaction of everyone. I am sure his department has done its best, but those who could not understand the labels were certainly not as well satisfied as those who did understand them. Of course, when you come to the question of a warning I understand, as the minister says, that many provincial laws cover the matter; yet we are legislating here in a federal parliament, and I thought for once I might convince my colleagues to take this step toward improving the situation and amend *the federal law as I suggest. The minister says the main thing is the provincial laws, and the care of people handling the drugs. It may be so partly, but we want to give them the assistance of having the labels printed in such a way that everyone can understand them. The minister later said the second point was the federal narcotics law, while the third point would be in regard to the labelling, but those are the two points I tried to cover in the bill. I should think it would .be only fair that some such provisions might be made to cover them, and I am really surprised that the minister does not agree with me on this question of the protection of a large part of the population.
With all due regard to the minister's ability, I am not convinced by his argument on these points to-night. However, as I admitted myself, the bill covers more than I at first intended, including food which I did not desire to cover and would need many amendments in committee, and since it can be brought back at another session-and I do not think this parliament will be dissolved before another session-I shall dream on it and redraft it in the hope that next year the idea may have gained way, its fairness may be recognized and it may be given more favourable consideration by the cabinet and the house. In these circumstances, Mr. Speaker,
I wish to withdraw the bill.

speechtext:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Income War Tax Act and to provide:
1. That for the 1947 and subsequent taxation years the present rules for computation of personal income tax be replaced by the following schedule of graduated rates:
On the first $250 of income or any portion thereof, 22 per cent per annum; or
$55 upon the income of $250; and 25 per cent upon the amount by which the income exceeds $250 and does not exceed $1,000; or
$242.50 upon the income of $1,000; and 28 per cent upon the amount by which the income exceeds $1,000 and does not exceed $2,500; or $662.50 upon the income of $2,500; and 31 per cent upon the amount by which the income exceeds $2,500 and does not exceed $4,500; or $1,282.50 upon the income of $4,500; and 34 per cent upon the amount by which the income exceeds $4,500 and does not exceed $6,500; or $1,962.50 upon the income of $6,500; and 38 per cent upon the amount by which the income exceeds $6,500 and does not exceed $8,500; or $2,722.50 upon the income of $8,500; and 42 per cent upon the amount by which the income exceeds $8,500 and does not exceed $10,500; or $3,562.50 upon the income of $10,500; and 46 per cent upon the amount by which the income exceeds $10,500 and does not exceed $13,000; or $4,712.50 upon the income of $13,000; and 50 per cent upon the amount by which the income exceeds $13,000 and does not exceed $18,000; or $7,212.50 upon the income of $18,000 and 55 per cent upon the amount by which the income exceeds $18,000 and does not exceed $30,000; or $13,812.50 upon the income of $30,000 and 60 per cent upon the amount by which the income exceeds $30,000 and does not exceed $50,000; or $25,812.50 upon the income of $50,000 and 65 per cent upon the amount by which the income exceeds $50,000 and does not exceed $70,000: or $38,812.50 upon the income of $70,000 and 70 per cent upon the amount by which the income exceeds $70,000 and does not exceed $100,000; or $59,812.50 upon the income of $100,000 and 75 per cent upon the amount by which the income exceeds $100,000 and does not exceed $150,000; or
$97,312.50 upon the income of $150,000 and 80 per cent upon the amount by which the income exceeds $150,000 and does not exceed $250,000; or
$177,312.50 upon the income of $250,000 and 85 per cent upon the amount by which the income exceeds $250,000.
I desire to offer a few observations in connection with the first three paragraphs of the resolution, dealing with the income tax on private individuals.

speakeroldname: Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Acting Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

speechtext:
I think I can agree with the minister when he says that the method of computation has been considerably simplified. I would go farther and say that any change made would be almost bound to simplify the difficult procedure which has grown up under the act of making computation of the tax.
However, the tax still has to be paid after the computation has been made, and it is for us to examine just what change has been made, and who has benefited by it. I find that 30 per cent of the revenue Obtained by the Dominion of Canada is obtained from personal income tax. Out of a total of $2,140 million the government expects to obtain from personal income tax the sum of $640 million. That is a substantial sum.
It is true that some 550,000 or 600,000 taxpayers will in the future not be bound to make out income tax returns. But a substantial number of low income taxpayers will still be bound to do so, and a substantial sum will be obtained from them. Taking the number of taxpayers in the report issued by the government for the year 1945, I estimate that 600,000 single men, each earning less than $1,500, will pay a total of S41 million; and
187.000	married men, wdthout children, each earning less than $2,000, will pay a total of $10 million. Then, 110,000 married men without children, each earning between $2,000 and $2,500, will pay a total of $14 million, and
100.000	married men with one child, each earning less than $2,500, will pay a total of $5 million.
In other words, single men still paying taxes and earning less than $1,500, and married men earning less than $2,500 will contribute toward the taxes of Canada approximately $70 million. I would say that is a substantial sum contributed by the men in the lower income tax brackets.
The minister has just said that the exemptions are the highest in the world. That may be true, so far as exemptions for single men are concerned, and perhaps it is true, but only by a narrow margin, for married men. But

it is not true so far as dependents are concerned, because in the United States the allowance for each dependent is $500, whereas in Canada, even taking the impact of family allowances into consideration, it has been figured out at approximately $300.
I must congratulate the officials of the income tax branch upon making out so well this list of percentages. It must have been done by a process of trial and error, because everything was arranged so that the allowance is practically equivalent to $300 for those in the lower income tax brackets. It gets slightly larger in those for higher incomes.
The people in the low income tax brackets who contribute this considerable sum of $70 million are also the people who contribute a great part of the other revenue.
It will be noticed that in introducing his budget the Minister of Finance pointed out, as indicated at page 2905 of Hansard, that we would receive $183 million from customs duties. I do not know why he estimated it so optimistically, because last year it was only $129 million. From the excise tax he expects to get $195 million, or slightly more than last year. Then, from the sales tax he expects $250 million, or an increase of about $38 million over the figure for the preceding year.
These people in the lower income tax brackets are the people with children, and they are the greatest buyers of the articles which are taxed in these other ways. The only taxes which to some extent they may escape are the corporate tax to an extent of $210 million, excess profits tax of $340 million, interest on dividends of $30 million, succession duties of $24 million and other miscellaneous taxes.
So that the people in the lower income tax brackets, those with large families, are still paying more than their fair share of the burden of taxation in Canada.
I believe I might now refer to paragraph (a) of resolution 3, where we find these words:
(a) Where the spouse has an income of more than $250 and less than $750 by the amount by which the spouse's income is more than $250.
That is, if a wife happens to go out and work her income will be deducted from her husband's exemption.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not wish to interrupt the hon. member, but if we might discuss that when we reach resolution 3 it would be helpful.

I shall leave that for the time being.
As I have said, the income tax will be responsible for 30 per cent of the revenue of Canada in the coming year. Yet this revenue will be dependent entirely upon the amount of

Income War Tax
wages the people in Canada will earn. I think the minister was optimistic when he estimated $620 million. I find that the total wage income for 1945 was about $5,200 million. That is a considerable sum, much more in fact than in the previous year, when it was only $4,790 million. I should think 1945 was a peak year. Let us go back to 1938, when the total income of wage-earners in Canada was $2,449 million. It was only $2,450 million in 1939 and in 1940. When we were having the effect of the war it was only as high as $2,860 million. Can anyone believe that wage-earners can pay $640 million out of income which may, and probably will, sink as low as that of 1940, which was a fair year? And yet, without this $640 million it will be extremely difficult to meet the ordinary expenses which are now over $1,200 million, and which are bound to increase in the future from the very fact that debt charges will increase, and the fact that, as it goes along, nearly every department of government is finding other ways of spending money.
It would be very pleasant if only the rich were to pay the taxes. I was interested to find from the government's own return that in 1945 which, to say the least, was a peak year, so far as earnings are concerned, only
17.000	people in the whole of Canada would acknowledge that they made over $10,000, and that only 7,800 of the 17,000 would admit that they made more than $15,000. One would almost think there must be something wrong. I would suppose there are hon. members in the house who might easily earn $10,000 a year. If they do, after they pay their taxes they must live in a humble and quiet way. Yet in Toronto-and I know only Toronto and these parliament buildings-there are many people who would seem to have more money than $10,000. Where do they get the money? If they are evading the income tax we should take measures to obtain it. If they are living on their capital, that is different. It may be that some of them are living on their capital because, as I recall it, attempts were made many years ago to estimate the wealth of different countries. At that time, in 1935, at the bottom of the depression the wealth of Canada was estimated at $25 billion. In 1928 it was estimated at $31 billion to $32 billion. What is it to-day? First of *all, we have a debt of $16 billion, and perhaps we ought to add that to the $32 billion, which would make us worth $48 billion, if these debts that we owe to one another are part of the capital of Canada. I realize that this is a more or less hit-or-miss way of estimating the wealth of the country; but the wealth of every country was estimated in that way, the wealth of Britain, France, and the United
States as so much, and the total wealth of Canada, as I say, was estimated at $32 billion at the highest point in our financial history. We might well stop and think that a country with a capital wealth of $32 billion and a debt of $16 billion requires drastic measures to reduce spending so that we may overtake this immense debt which we have. I know it is an internal debt that we owe to one another, and only a very small portion of it is external debt, but it all has to be met so far as the individual taxpayer is concerned.
I should like to say something about the trade of Canada. Everybody is always speaking of the necessity of Canada having foreign trade. I was surprised to see in the monthly review of statistics some figures as to the trade of Canada during the month of April last. Those are the most recent figures I have, although I believe that the minister had more recent figures. They have not come to me, nor are they in the library. I have not the very latest figures; I wish I had. I find that during the first four months of this year, according to the figures I have, the imports of Canada amounted to $555 million and our exports, $700 million. The exports are very fine, but how do our imports compare with those of the last eight months of 1945? The imports for the first four months of 1946 were $555 million and the imports for the last eight months of 1945 were $1,215 million. The exports during the first four months of 1946 were only $700 million, as compared with exports of $2,250,000 during the last eight months of 1945. In other words, a credit of one billion dollars in the last eight months of 1945 has dropped to a credit balance of less than $150,000,000 during the first four months of this year.
We must live on our exports. That is our profit, and our profit is fast receding according to the figures of our exports for the present year. We know a lot of our exports are goods that we are sending out of the country by way of gifts. I am not criticizing that, but since we are giving away a lot of our goods I say that we should have a large surplus of exports over imports. During the last eight months of 1945 we had a favourable balance of trade of $160,000,000 with the United States. During the first four months of this year we have an unfavourable balance of trade of approximately $150,000,000 with the United States so that we are very likely in the near future, if this trend goes on, to owe to the United States a large external debt which will have to be paid. We shall have to raise the money.

Does that unfavourable
trade balance make allowance for our gold shipments?
Income War Tax

I do not think so. I think that is trade pure and simple. Any gold which we might export to the United States would hardly be for that amount, unless several years' accumulation were sent over at once. The largest amount of gold that we sent out of Canada in the most favourable year, as I recollect, would be about $200,000,000.
As I was saying, we shall have to raise the money. My suggestion to the government is that there must be other means of raising it than by taxing such a large percentage of the people's earnings. There is no doubt in the world that many people hesitate to work when in the case of a single man everything he earns over $750 is to be taxed at the rate of 22 per cent. The minister in his budget speech did not give the rates in other countries, but the Minister of National Health and Welfare covered that in his fifteen points-one more than President Wilson had-and he spoke of the larger exemptions that were allowed in Canada. But he did not mention how much higher our rates were, once the exemptions were taken care of. I find that the rates in the United States start at 17 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: At 19 per cent, I think.

The extra three per cent might bring it up to 19 per cent. I think the minister is correct. The rates in the United States then start at 19 per cent and ours start at 22 per cent. The rate is important to the man who pays the tax, much more important than the few dollars of exemption which he is allowed. I would say to the government that some other method of raising the large sum of money required must be found than simply taking the earnings of the people which they have acquired by hard work. There is not enough differentiation made between the man who earns his money by hard labour and the man whose income comes from investments which were acquired at a time when there was no large income tax. I cannot conceive of anybody ever becoming wealthy under our present income tax laws, especially on earnings from personal work. To-day we had before us a bill to raise judges' salaries, and I sat down with a pencil and figured that every dollar that we gave them in increased salaries amounted approximately to their income tax. So that their only hope of being able to get some personal benefit from the increase is in the reduction of the income tax. A man who makes $20,000 a year will pay $7,000 in income tax under this budget, and anybody who earns less than that has little or no prospect of ever being anything but a poor man. The difference between the wealthy 
and the poor will, as the years go by, be accentuated under the tax laws such as we now have before us.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
When I spoke in the
main budget debate I devoted a good portion of my remarks to the schedule which is proposed in this first resolution, and I made it my contention that it was an unfair schedule on the ground that it gave more substantial relief to those in the upper brackets than to those in the lower income brackets. In support of my argument I gave the house four tables, which are found in Hansard at pages 3374 and 3375. I indicated in connection with each of these tables that my purpose in giving them was to substantiate my contention in different ways. My point was that whether one considered the net increase in "take-home pay" or the grading of the income tax rates into the upper brackets, or if one made comparisons with the past-and I took the particular year 1941 for reasons I gave- in all cases the point wras substantiated that relief was greater for those in the upper brackets than for those in the lower income brackets.
My reason for rising to say a few words on this matter at this time is that when the Minister of Finance spoke in this debate on July 18 he did me the honour of paying some attention to the argument which I had made and to the tables which I had presented. I was not terribly surprised that he did not agree with the social philosophy behind my contentions, but there are some remarks I feel I must make with respect to his comments on my tables, particularly one of them which I shall come to in a moment.
First of all, the minister said as reported at page 3591 of Hansard-.
Whether his first table-
Referring to mine.
-has any validity or not is a matter of political philosophy, more than anything else.
Mr. Knowles:	Social philosophy.
Mr. Ilsley:	Social philosophy, perhaps. But
I disagree so fundamentally - with the whole basis of the argument he used that I do not think I need say anything further to indicate that fact.
Obviously it is difficult for us to get together there, but it is also clear that we are in that case arguing, not the rightness or wrongness of figures, but rather a difference in social philosophy. My contention was somewhat along the lines of the views advanced by the previous speaker, namely, that, when revising the income tax structure, more consideration should be given to those who need it most, namely those in the lower brackets. Then the minister said, with refer-

Income War Tax
ence to my second and third tables which are found on page 3374 of Hansard for July 11:
The second and third tables are difficult to . understand, and they do not indicate that there have not been substantial tax reductions.
Well, I never claimed for these tables that they do not indicate that there have been substantial tax reductions; the very opposite was the case. In fact, reference back to page 3373 will show that I said this:
It will be perfectly clear to lion, members when they look at these tables that the grading up of the rates ivas steeper under the old system than it will be under the new.
That was my point in presenting these tables, to indicate that there had been reductions all right, but that these reductions are more substantial in the upper brackets than is the case in the lower groups. That, therefore, was the purpose of these tables, even though the minister found it difficult to understand them. I really think that behind that statement was the position he intimated earlier, namely a difference in social philosophy.
However, I might not have bothered to take the time of the committee to reply to the minister if it were not for the criticism he made of my fourth table which appears at page 3375 of Hansard for July 11. This is what the minister had to say, at least in part:
Then, I wish to refer to the fourth table particularly, because of the rather striking statement by the hon. member as it is found at page 3373 of Hansard where it says-
And then the minister read a fairly lengthy quotation from my speech which I do not think it necessary for me to requote at this time. Having done that, the minister went

I said, when the tables were placed on Hansard, that I would not raise any objection to them, but that there was no admission as to the correctness of them. Even if I share some of the principles of social philosophy of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre I cannot agree with him when he says that reductions in income tax this year are more important for upper income brackets than for lower income brackets. Before dealing with that, I think that we can agree on these principles of social philosophy. According to social justice, there are two main principles in taxation. The first one is that all government bodies must measure taxes to adminin-istrative needs. That is a duty and we must fulfil it even in spite of demagogic opposition. The general evolution in the world and in our country requires higher and higher budgets as far as ordinary expenses are concerned. My hon. friends who sit just in front of me will agree with that, and they are asking for more social security, and thus for higher budgets. The increase in population, the constant evolution in the world and social security add every year to the responsibility of the state. I do not see how we can go back; we must go forward. We cannot go back; we must follow progress. The greater the field of government action, the more numerous must be its administrative staff and the more effective must be the administration. All that requires more money. That means more taxes. Let us consider the question of taxes with a true civic spirit, having in mind-and I think it is important-that the income tax is the best way for the equitable distribution of wealth.
The second principle of social justice in taxation is that taxes must be proportionate to the citizen's resources. That is the principle I want to study and the application of which I want to look for in the resolutions of the budget we are now studying.
I said last year that taxes should be imposed on personal income only over and above the minimum necessary to each one, according to his own family responsibilities. What is strictly necessary for an individual or for an individual and his family must be exempted. What has been called the normal tax takes away from the citizen in the lower brackets of income what is strictly necessary. Such a tax is unfair and unjust, and I am sure that the people of Canada are satisfied that it will disappear.
What is the amount strictly necessary for a married couple to live in Canada at the present time, and what is the amount necessary to raise children? I say, the government's obligations being what they are, the total of such amounts, according to the needs of each individual, should be the non-compressible revenue for that individual.

Income War Tax
At the present time what is the average cost in Canada of the necessities of life for a married couple? I could not find any statistics in this connection. I inquired of the proper authorities, and the only statistics indicated to me were those giving the estimated distribution of income recipients by income classes for 1942, which can be found in the appendix to a publication of the dominion bureau	of statistics entitled,
"National accounts, income and expenditures, 1938-1945." Table 2A of the appendix gives the estimated distribution of income recipients by income classes for 1942, excluding agriculture and the armed services. I submit that in order to obtain an average we can take this table, because on the one hand the revenue of the farmers is difficult to calculate or appreciate, for obvious reasons, and on the other hand1 the income of persons in the armed services in 1942 was only temporary. The table gives the number of married men in the various income classes without distinction between those who have children and those who have not. I took an average as accurately as I could and arrived at the figure of $1,441 a year as the average income of married men in Canada in 1942. I was unpleasantly surprised to find the [DOT] figure so low, which goes to prove that the people with lower incomes must be protected and that their incomes should be increased by all means possible under present economic conditions. Since 1942 there has been an increase of about twenty per cent, which would give for married men in Canada in 1946 an estimated average income of $1,730 a year.
Let us assume that this figure is the average income of a married man in Canada in 1946. We may say that it contains, first, what is strictly necessary for his wife and himself; second, for an average of a little more than two children; third, that it includes also the income tax paid in 1942 and also the savings that were made, without counting any luxuries. If you take off all the other items, the total of what is strictly necessary for the married man and his wife will fall below $1,500. That is as accurate as I can get it with the figures at hand; and $1,500 is the exemption proposed in the budget resolution. I repeat that I am far from sure the amount is accurate, and I would urge the Minister of Finance, or the acting minister, to have a survey made every five years-and I think this is important-to learn the average cost of living in the cities of Canada in order to determine what is necessary to maintain single persons and married couples, and then children of various ages, 63260-238
so that after each period' the exemptions may be revised accordingly. I said we should ascertain the average cost of living in the cities, because if we took a complete average it would mean an average of the whole country, which in turn would mean that the population of the cities, where the cost of living is highest, would be called upon to pay taxes on part of what is strictly necessary for their maintenance.
I now come to the children. I said last fall, and I repeat, that what is strictly necessary to rear a child should not be taxable. Here again we have no statistics for Canada. However, in 1938 a survey was made in the United States, and it was found that the annual cost of feeding and clothing children from one to eighteen years of age varied from $109.40 to $241.60. As I say, these figures include only the cost of food and clothing. If you add $125 as an average to cover the other expenses, and to cover also the difference between the cost of living in the United States in 1938 and the cost of living in Canada in 1946, you will arrive at an average of around $300. which is the exemption proposed for children in the present resolution.
As a matter of fact, taking into account the family allowance, the exemption is more than $300, especially in the lower income brackets. For instance, take a man with five children, earning $3,000 a year. If the exemption for his children was $300 each he would have an exemption of $1,500 for his wife and himself and $1,500 for his children. He would receive nothing and would have no tax to pay. Under the present system, however, his exemption for himself and his wife will be $1,500 and his exemptions for his five children will be $100 each or $500, which makes a total exemption of $2,000, leaving a taxable income of $1,000 on which his tax is $242.50. On the other hand, however, he will receive at least $312 in family allowances. Consequently his net income at the end of the year will be $3,069.50, all taxes paid; and that is a man with an income of $3,000. Not only will he have no tax to pay; he will have a surplus of $69.50 over his earned income. Take a man with five children, earning $2,000 a year. He will have no tax to pay. His exemption is $2,000, and he will receive $312 in family allowances. Who said the new system is not protecting families in the lower income brackets? Who will say that even with the tremendous expenses it has to meet the government'is not giving to all, under the circumstances, a great measure of equality of opportunity? I congratulate the Minister of Finance on having set up a system of

Income War Tax

personal income tax which protects the families, especially in the lower income brackets, and which imposes a tax only on the available income of the taxpayer after the necessities of life have been provided, according to his needs.
Before I go on, I should like to say a few words about the exemptions for children going to college or university. I submit that there should be no age limit of twenty-one and, in addition, that the cost of sending a son or daughter to university is so much more than S300 a year that a man should be allowed to deduct the actual expenses incurred in the education of his son or daughter falling within that category. Let him produce receipts, if necessary, but give him a chance. Taxpayers of average means cannot afford such advanced education for their children. However, I submit that those children have the same right of education that the children of rich men have. The interest of the state itself is to have the greatest possible number of advanced and educated men, and its corollary duty is to encourage young people and their parents to do so, in giving all classes of society equality of opportunity in that field.
Now that there have been corrected the two great injustices of the normal tax and of the uniform imposition of the graduated rates over $1,200, and now that there has been applied the sound principle of net incompressible income, according to family responsibilities, let us see what should be the distribution of the personal income tax on what is left over and above that minimum.
A distribution of justice requires that the rates be graduated. Let me only recall what the Master said about the poor widow. I am sure I do not have to mention to hon. members that passage in scripture which refers to the poor widow who had put only one penny into the fund, but was declared to have been the one who had given the greatest alms. As to the scale of rates, it should depend upon the needs of the state. 'There is no doubt that the rates proposed in the resolution are high. But the needs of the state are also very high and will still be in 1947. Let us hope that reductions will be announced in the next year's budget, and that such reductions will be made, especially in the lower rates of the scale, so as to ensure better distribution of wealth, and to promote further equality of opportunity.

This allowance, which quite substantially exceeds $108 per child, which most people assumed it would be, arises from the following provisions in the act:

On the whole, the tax value of Children for incomes of over $4,500 in families of six children and over, is lower under the new law than under the old one. In most cases this difference is more than offset by the reduction in the total tax to which the parent is liable; but in a few cases the decrease in the tax value of the child is greater than the reduction in income tax that would otherwise occur. Consequently there is no reduction of tax, on balance.
To explain it with figures, the tax value of children for 1946, owing to the reasons I have mentioned, in a family of six children is as follows: $432 on an income of $1,200; only a few dollars more on $2,000; only a few dollars more on from $3,000 to $3,500; $550-on $4,000, and a little over $600 on an income of $4,500. Then it goes up sharply, reaching $1,100 at an income of $8,000.
In 1947 that line is levelled, and the tax value of the same children varies from $560 at an income of $2,100 to about $650 at an income of $8,000. The line for 1947 crosses the 1946 line at an income of $4,500, the tax value being there, I repeat, a little over $600.
All that means that justice has been done to everyone, that a disproportionate tax value for children has disappeared for higher incomes in that category, and that a fair and levelled tax value has been given to children in large families with incomes below $4,500. For the very few cases in which the net position in 1947 is worse than in 1946, I wonder if it would not be possible to have a proviso that in no case would anyone be asked to pay more income tax in 1947, after due deduction of the amount of the family allowances received,, than he will have paid in 1946, in the same-conditions of income and family obligations. It is only a few dollars, and if I were one who, upon filling out my income tax, found that in the same conditions and with the same income I w'ould have a few dollars more to pay, I would not be pleased; that is certain.

If I had to pay more I would get mad and I believe that a few taxpayers will certainly get mad.
Many hon. members have spoken of the failure of the government to raise the exemptions for the lower incomes sufficiently high. I have already dealt with that, but let me add that with a population of 4,500,000 gainfully employed in Canada, only 1,800,000, or a little more than one-third, will pay personal income tax. I do not say that those exemptions could not be raised, but if they are they should be raised when it is also possible to reduce the rates of the graduated tax, especially on those with lower incomes.
Let us take examples which will show that for lower incomes the reduction is important. I have already given some for incomes of $2,000 and $3,000, with five children. Let us now take a man with an income of $2,250 and two children under sixteen years of age. For 1946, his net tax after receiving family allowances will be $72. In 1947-I am not making a comparison with 1941 because that is too far away and I think it is more fair to compare 1946 with 1947-his family allowances will exceed his income tax by $14. That is more than a reduction; he will have no tax to pay and will be actually $14 better off in earned income.
A man whose income is $2,500 and has three *children -under sixteen, will in 1947 pay $167.50 in taxes, but he will receive $194 in family allowances. His net position, therefore, at the end of the year will be a net income of $2,527.50. He will be better off in earned income by $27.50.
All the examples that one can take go to prove that, even with the high rates of graduated tax, we have attained a great measure of equality of opportunity in applying sound principles. Let us hope that with further reductions in the rates when government expenses fall, we shall attain a full measure of equality of opportunity.

Before this section carries, I should like to draw the attention of the acting minister to something which I think works hardship and injustice on certain employees. Perhaps I can explain this best by giving a specific instance. The one which was drawn to my attention was the case of a girl teaching in a country school who, in the course of events, submitted the amount of her income on the proper form to the department. At the same time her income was returned to the income tax department as being so much; I refer to the return on the form-I believe it is T.D.-l-which the employer uses to inform the department of the amount earned by the employee. The secretary of the school district in which the girl was working supplied his estimate of the amount of her income. She disputed that amount; she wrote to the school board and asked that it be corrected, but for some reason this was not done. I believe the secretary simply adopted the attitude that he had already finished with that matter and that as far as be -was concerned he could not be bothered about it. So the girl was informed by the income tax department's local office that the only thing they had before them was the amount furnished by the employer, and since she was an interested party they could not accept her figure. However, they advised her to write to the employer and get the correct figure. Again she wrote and this time no notice was taken of the letter. The result was that the income tax people threatened to sue that girl for the amount and they had her frightened to such an extent that she paid the full amount although she knew she had not earned the income on which the amount was based. Rather than get into trouble she paid the extra amount. It was then that I received a letter about the matter, and it was finally straightened out so that she was given the refund and the matter was adjusted. I thought it was my duty to bring such a case to the attention of the income tax people in the hope that some provision might be made-I do not know how; that is their headache-to prevent that type of injustice occurring again where the employer is not willing to cooperate with the employee and with the income tax department.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That would be a very rare case. Of course, the income tax inspector, or whoever it was, had no right to insist upon taking the return of the employer rather than the statement made by the young lady in her income tax return that that was her income. In the result, as my hon. friend has pointed out, the situation was cleared up and the

Income War Tax
refund made. She is only liable to pay tax on her real income. If the employer makes a mistake and reports on T.D.-1, if that is the number of the form, that the income was in excess of the amount actually received, the mistake is his and not the taxpayer's, and the taxpayer is entitled to insist that the tax be paid only on the income actually received. This young lady no doubt did take appropriate steps later on to see that she was not charged more than she should be. It is one of the things incidental to administration. The law is perfectly clear. The taxpayer files his return and pays tax on that. If the return is incorrect the department is entitled to assess. It is not a case of the employer's word against the taxpayer's, but a question of what the amount actually received by the taxpayer was.

There is no way, as far
as I can find out or can presently see, for the department to ascertain what the actual figure was. If the employer has given a wrong statement and refuses to give another, who is to decide what the amount was?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

If the department under
those circumstances insists on taking the employer's word as against the taxpayer's, the taxpayer has the simple recourse of filing an appeal within thirty days under the provisions of the act, and that takes the form of a simple letter appealing against the assessment. The appeal is to the minister and it would come in the ordinary course to the department at Ottawa. It would come to the attention of the deputy minister and the matter would be investigated. I think the case mentioned by my hon. friend, while it is an accurate statement of what took place in the circumstances, is exceedingly rare, because I suppose 999 employers out of 1,000 file correct statements showing the amount actually paid to the employee, and it is hard to imagine a case where it is called to the attention of the employer that he appears to have made a mistake that he would refuse to correct it or to reply to a letter. But that is one of the hazards incident to human nature.

The hon. member for Peterborough West referred to interest charged on arrears where such arrears arise in consequence of an error in calculating the amount of the tax. What I have to say in that regard arises out of certain representations made to me by farmer organizations. As the minister is aware, the farmers of western Canada are at the present time just a bit disturbed, to put it mildly. Their feeling is not attributable entirely to matters relating to income tax. There is the price structure in relation to costs,
over which the minister has no control. There is the cost of living, about which of course they are disturbed, because they have no faith whatsoever in the cost of living index, which ignores taxes, and quality or lack of quality of clothing, and so forth. There is some complaint about having to file tax returns. However, they knew that the law obliges them to file returns and that a day of reckoning would arrive. Therefore I am not saying anything about that argument of theirs. Many of them, however, make this statement: "We worked under extreme difficulties during the war when there were shortages, more particularly shortages of skilled help. We put in long hours, up to sixteen a day. We are not skilled in the art of completing income tax returns and often we have no time to go to points where satisfactory help could be secured. We did our best in computing the returns and we submitted them. We heard nothing about them for two or three years, and then we were advised that we had miscalculated and therefore owed the department one, two or three hundred dollars, and were charged five per cent on balances due."
The argument of the income tax branch has been this: "We have experienced a shortage of staff." Well, the farmer's argument is just a3 legitimate. The income tax people say, "We have inexperienced help," but the farmer was in exactly the same position. The farmer says, "These people have a specific task, namely, that of assessing returns, and we feel that we should not be penalized in consequence of their taking two or three years to notify us that we owe them two or three hundred dollars." Some got their 1943 assessments last year; some got their 1942 assessments last year, and personally I feel that they have a legitimate argument in asking for consideration as far as interest on unpaid returns is concerned.
The argument might be advanced that they are assessed interest only as from the date of assessment. That was what the minister was going to say, I have no doubt.

I should like to say a few words in respect of the exemption for income tax purposes. We fully appreciate, as has been argued, that the government is in great need of revenue. Of course it is difficult for the single man who receives $14.50 a week to understand why he is still going to pay taxes on that amount. The government says to him, "Well, we need the revenue." Of course he advances this argument, and more particularly in some parts of Canada, "It certainly was not because of our advice that you used financial methods which piled up the colossal debt, colossal interest charges plus the other colossal fixed commitments, and all the other commitments that resulted." It is small consolation to the single man who receives $15 or $16 a week to be told whenever he encounters difficulties in getting along, "Just think of the government's great needs which are still greater than yours."
So far as the married man is concerned, if he receives $28.80 or $29 a week he is taxed.
I do not know just what argument could be advanced, especially with the present increased living costs, and the higher taxes in every field including those on his own home, to convince this man that he should be taxed. It is hard for any of us to accept the argument that because of the great needs of the country we must retain our exemptions at such an extremely low level. Personally I gave a great deal of consideration to the demand for a $1,000 exemption for the single man and $2,000 for the married man.
I stuck at it, simply because I have made certain budget calculations. I am not going to quote any figures, but it is an application of a bit of common sonso to our living costs of to-day as compared with three, four or five years ago. The worst feature of it is 
that the cost of living is sky-rocketing to-day. That is taking place in spite of the controls. Any man who pays a bill will realize that his general cost of living has increased materially. He cannot be kidded by any 122 or 124 as the cost of living index. For example, the commodities of food and clothing make up the bulk of the purchases of the family man. So far as clothing is concerned, I say that the cost of living has gone up more than forty per cent, and the cost of foodstuffs generally has gone up an equivalent amount. To ask or to expect that we shall maintain in this country a decent standard of health and a proper mental outlook, while at the same time still imposing upon the $14 a week single man and the $28 married man these high rates of taxation, is to kid ourselves.
I do not wish to take up any more time at this moment, except to say that with respect to interest I shall watch the resolution referred to and if it does not grant the concessions which we believe the farmers are entitled to then I shall be obliged to occupy more of the time of the committee.

Before this section is carried,
I should like to refer once again to the question that is puzzling farmers to a great extent in my part of the country, namely taxation on money received from the sale of grain grown in the early years of the war. The farmers were compelled to store this grain because of the quota system which was in effect. Then, when the grain was sold in 1943, 1944 or 1945 they are compelled to pay taxes on the basis of the year the grain was sold rather than when the grain was grown.
I should like to have a statement from the minister in that connection. I feel that if the grain was grown in 1940 and was stored because of the quota system in effect, which was not the choice of the farmer but of the government, then the grain should be assessed at the 1940 rate rather than that of 1944 or some other subsequent year when the grain was sold.
I shall look into the question raised by the hon. member.
