In fixing the exemption for single people at $750, has the department ever endeavoured to analyse just how difficult it is for a single person to live in a city on that amount. May I suggest here that it is to a large extent in the cities where the income tax is most easily collected. The income tax is often said to be the ideal tax, but may I say to the minister that the income taxes are satisfactory only where books are kept and where there is an accounting. There are a great many people in Canada as a whole who do not receive their salaries from a corporation or business, and it is not so easy to ascertain whether or not they do have incomes. I sometimes believe that we put an overemphasis on income tax as the ideal form of tax. Perhaps there are other forms which are worthy of more attention than they receive.
To get back to the original suggestion as to whether or not the Department of National Revenue or the Department of Finance ever investigated the difficulty of an individual single person living in a city like Toronto or Montreal on the minimum exemption of $750 63260-239
which is allowed under section 2, I have had a budget prepared by a young woman, in fact, by my secretary in Toronto, which is entitled "Cost of Living Chart for a Single Girl on a Weekly Basis." I think it is worthy of presentation to this committee because it does show-and I think the committee can pass on it as well as any person-whether or not an individual can live on this small sum of money, $750, before being subject to the first bracket of taxation of 22 per cent.
The budget is as follows: board and room for the week, $8. I do not think anyone will cavil at that amount being set aside for a single girl living in a large city. Car tickets, $1, which would provide just enough to take her to and from work, I think with one extra trip a week. Lunches, $2; that is, 40 cents a working day for lunch. Some people may think that is high for an average lunch, but occasion-; ally they want a bit of variety, so that I do not think anyone will object to that.
That is very low.

I think so myself, but I shall leave it to the committee. This budget was drawn up on October 24 last, and no doubt prices have risen since then. Clothing, $4 a week; and I see in parenthesis, "and incidentals necessary to good grooming." Then doctor and dentist bills, including medicines, tooth paste and so on, $1. I see there is a note on this item, which says:
Most people in ordinary circumstances go far too long without consulting their doctor; in fact it could safely be said that the majority wait until they experience symptoms of illness rather than have the necessary check-up. So to build up 'a needed reserve for doctor bills, hospital expenses, to take care of periodic check-ups with the dentist and to provide the necessary aids to good health, $52 a year seems little enough.
Then there is entertainment, club fees, educational and cultural advancement, at fifty cents a week. I do not think anyone will object to a small amount like that. Next is a rather large item which is perhaps not often met with: church collection and donations, fifty cents a week. We can cut that out entirely if hon. members wish; it is only $25 a year and would not do very much to disprove the point I am endeavouring to make, but personally I think most of us feel that fifty cents is not a large amount for church collection and donations, and certainly it is very much less than the tithe some people like to contribute. Then there is an item for a holiday fund, to provide for the two weeks it is hoped to get as holidays, which requires the saving of $1 a week throughout the year; and it is difficult to get holidays nowadays even for $50. These items total $18 a week; on a yearly basis the total

Income War Tax

is $936, or $186 over the exemption of $750. I believe, after an examination of the individual items, hon. members will feel that they are on the low side rather than the high side. There is a deficiency, therefore, of $186 below the amount which I think can be considered a minimum; but if a person does earn $936 to cover this minimum budget the tax collector comes around and collects 22 per cent on the amount in excess of $750, or a total of $40.92, which I feel is too much to take from a person in that income bracket.
I shall not go into the budget for a married person endeavouring to live on $1,500 in one of our cities, but it is impossible to maintain anything like a Canadian standard on such a minimum amount of money. I wonder whether or not the tax collectors in setting such minimum amounts, have really examined the position of these people. It is quite true they come back and tell you that we are now carrying on a great many social services and that there are other expenses-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: They are the most generous exemptions in the world.

Let us assume that our
exemptions are the most generous in the world, as the minister has said. I shall not challenge his statement, but I wonder whether many of the things the government has undertaken are really wanted by the people who are just above these exemption brackets of $750 and $1,500; whether these people really want the things the government is endeavouring to provide for them, or the other things on which the government spends the taxpayers' money. It would not be so bad to provide all the things w'e do provide, to spend all this money on information services, film boards and everything else we think may be desirable, though expensive, if the taxes could be collected from those whose standard of living is not brought below' a minimum which any member of this committee would consider decent. Therefore I feel that when the house is appropriating money we should realize that a large part of our revenue comes from single people who are just above the $750 bracket and from married people just above the $1,500 bracket. The government continually remind us of the amount of revenue that would be lost if the exemptions were raised to more reasonable standards. But I hope they realize that they are taxing people below what could be considered sufficient to maintain what we believe to be a minimum standard of living; and I suggest that we cut down expenses on many of the things on which we are spending the money of these poor taxpayers, these things and services which are not as necessary to 
them as is a little higher standard of living. That is one of the reasons why many on this side of the house feel that some better treatment should be given Canadian taxpayers in the very low brackets, by way of further exemptions.

Ever since the minister delivered his budget speech, I have been thinking that in 1941 Roosevelt and Churchill met somewhere in the Atlantic and agreed to an Atlantic charter. Two of the things against which the world was supposed to be guaranteed in that charter were want and fear. What we have succeeded in doing is guaranteeing to all of us want and fear. This is a most astonishing thing. From coast to coast in this country I believe the people are just haunted by want and fear.
The remarks of the hon. member for Rose-dale would cause almost anyone to think seriously along this line. The hon. member could have gone on to point out several other things which are being overlooked. Let us suppose that a young girl finishes high school, goes to normal and then commences to teach. Let us suppose she has accumulated a debt of $300 in order to complete her education. This girl starts to work, we will say, at $750 or $800 a year. Suppose she cuts down the expenses mentioned by the hon. member for Rosedale by twenty-five per cent. In the first place, let the most brilliant man in the income tax department go to work and figure out how long it will take that girl to pay off her $300 debt. Then, let him figure out how long it will take her to save enough to provide for two or three years of additional education. In the case of a young man, how long will it take to prepare himself to be able to marry? How long will it take either the girl or the young man to provide anything like sufficient savings for their later years? In case this girl has an accident or must have an operation for appendicitis, costing perhaps $125, with a doctor bill of, say $100, how long will it take to pay off those bills?
I do not want to complain overmuch, but I think we are seriously neglecting a large percentage of the population to whom we ought to be giving careful attention. If we are going to impoverish the youth of the land and destroy their incentive, how shall we build that fine, high morale, which should prevail to make this a great nation? How shall we build in our young people a confidence that Canada is really the great land we all supposed she was?
Some serious thought must be given to this matter. It may be argued that the government must have money. I grant that, freely.

Income War Tax
My own ideas as to where money can come from are well enough known to hon. members. I find that in a general way, when those ideas are even mentioned, the minds of hon. members close up, just like granite. It is high time members of the house began to open their minds a bit. Surely what can be achieved in the way of social services and many other things that are desirable, surely the extent of those services is not going to be limited by the amount of dollars we can wring out of our people by such oppressive taxation as is now inflicted upon them.
It ought to be clear to hon. members that to suppose that such a limit is the governing factor is only to be foolish. It is time there was different thinking in financial circles of this countiy. It is time we began to realize that the amount of money we can have depends upon the goods and services we can produce, and not upon the dollars we can wring out of the people's pockets.
If members of the Progressive Conservative party would begin to direct their attention along those lines instead of talking about economy all the time-[DOT]

I am listening.
Mr. BLACIvMORE: -they would be on their way to real progress. If their thinking and their expressions should follow along the line that what is physically possible in this country must be made financially possible-
That is too much to expect.

-and if the Liberals would begin to think along the same lines they would begin to say, "That is good, sound, common sense. What is physically possible ought to be financially possible. How can we make that come about?" Then I think we would begin to look upon as a monstrosity such taxation measures as we are at present seriously contemplating in this House of Commons.
It may be argued that we have the most generous taxation system to be found. Well, that is no credit to us. The serious thing is the way we are afflicting the people who make this country their home. I believe I have said enough for the present. I shall probably have more to say later on.

There are only four minutes to go, and I was wondering if I might use them by trying to say something sensible. I am inspired to speak, not by the hon. member for Lethbridge but by the hon. member for Rosedale. We both agree on one thing, namely that the exemptions in the lower income tax 63260-239i
brackets are too low-. If I understood the hon. member correctly, that is about the extent to which we agree, for the thesis he propounded was that people were kept poor because of the taxes they pay. If the hon. member takes the tax on an income of 8900 or $800 at 22 per cent he will find that it is a small amount. No one is made poor because that amount is taken from him. He was made poor long before that happened. And he is kept poor, not because he is taxed, but because he does not get the full or the social value of his production. That is why he is poor.
We are not going to remedy the position, either, by making things financially possible that are physically possible, or by eliminating taxes, until we get down to the fact that a man is entitled to a living simply because he is a human being. And he is entitled to a living on an equality with all other -human beings in the country, because the wealth of the country cannot be produced without him and his kind. We have on our hands some labour disputes, in which a great many people are involved. These are people with small incomes. But when they stop working, the wealth out of which comes all income is not produced.
I agree with the hon. member for Rosedale that the exemptions are too low. But when I included that in an amendment to the budget, he voted against it, just as he and his colleagues voted against the various other things which the leader of the opposition supported to-day, but which- he voted against last week.
We must stop talking on both sides of our face. We must deal with issues as they really are, and not in the superficial way that my hon. friends are dealing with them.
Resolution stands.
Progress reported.
